about: Every input of the cultivated-meat model (inputs.py REGISTRY), generated by agents_edition.py. value is the point value the model uses; range is the Monte Carlo prior (triangular: lo, mode, hi; lognormal: median mode, lo and hi the 5th and 95th percentiles; null: fixed). evidence_class is read mechanically from the source tag. moves_cost and moves_share appear for the inputs answer_rests_on.py finds move the cost by $1 a kilo or the share by its thresholds when set to each end of their range.

evidence_classes.setting: a setting of the model or a design choice, not an estimate
evidence_classes.judgement: a judgement or assumption of the model, not measured
evidence_classes.fitted: fitted to data: the model solves it so that it reproduces an observed figure
evidence_classes.derived: derived by arithmetic from published figures
evidence_classes.company: a company's or a vendor's figure, not peer reviewed
evidence_classes.published_partly: a published figure, read only in part (a snippet, an abstract or a second-hand citation)
evidence_classes.published: a published or observed figure (a paper, a report read in full, a market price, official statistics)

inputs.name: markup_add
inputs.source: [USDA ERS fit, judgement] per-kg costs from harvested cells to the shop shelf (forming, packing, cold chain, distribution, store handling). The shelf price is (cost + markup_add) / (1 - retail_margin). Fitting that form with a 28% retail margin to USDA ERS 2025 retail and wholesale values gives $1.6/kg for broilers, $2.9 for Choice beef and $3.5 for pork (pork's retail basket includes cured bacon and ham); cultivated cells also need dewatering and forming (au_processing, about $1).
inputs.note: CHANGED 2026-11-18 from a flat $5 (range 3-8.7) that stood for the WHOLE wholesale-to-retail spread. The spread has a per-kg part (retail moves about dollar for dollar with wholesale prices over 1-5 years, USDA ERS monthly 1970-2025) and a percentage part (retailers' gross margin), now `retail_margin`. research_notes/retail_markup_form.md. Setting retail_margin to 0 and this to 5 gives the old flat rule.

inputs.name: retail_margin
inputs.source: [Progressive Grocer ~2011 (snippet); Cooperative Grocer 2016 (read); OFPM 2025 via Reussir (read)] the retailer's gross margin on fresh meat, as a share of the shelf price: US meat departments 27.6% and 28-32%; French supermarkets 25% on a premium Label Rouge chicken, 36% on a chicken fillet, 48% on pork loin.
inputs.note: ADDED 2026-11-18. A percentage of the shelf price, so a dearer product carries a larger margin in dollars. Held constant across products: the French data show premium chicken at a LOWER percentage than the standard fillet but more euros per kg; claims that premium tiers carry higher percentages (up to about 40%) set the upper end. research_notes/retail_markup_form.md.

inputs.name: p_conv
inputs.source: [market] conventional commodity meat price (~$10-15/kg)
inputs.note: PIVOTAL: co-sets the parity threshold, p_conv * (1 - retail_margin) - markup_add (a meat tax enters here).

inputs.name: overhead
inputs.source: [SuperMeat, capital restated] everything except medium. Running costs as the company reports them, $10.8/kg ($11.8/lb 'without depreciation' = $26.0/kg, less 30.5 L x $0.50 of medium), plus a full yearly charge on the plant, $8.3/kg
inputs.note: RANGE moved 2026-11-21 (13.8-34.0 before) with the plant ladder: lo is plant_floor, hi the half-density tier, now explore() itself. THE PLANT knob. CAPITAL: the report gives depreciation of $1.6/lb ($3.5/kg) but neither the plant's cost nor the depreciation period. Assuming straight-line over 10 years (Humbird's plant life), the plant costs $35 per kg of yearly output, and at the 23.6%-a-year charge used for every other case (humbird_plant_charge) that is $8.3/kg. Over 20 years it would be $16.7/kg. The company's own figure with depreciation only is $29.5/kg in all; this default is $34.3. CAUTION: the report's stated tank volumes, densities and bleed rate reproduce about half its stated output, so its plant cost per kg cannot be checked. lo=13.8 = the plant floor (floor_physics: no clean rooms, perfusion, efficient cells; it was 10.8 until 2026-11-20, when plant_floor moved to what the engine gives, and is not the company's $10.8 of running costs above, which it happened to equal). hi=34 = the cautious case with cells at half the density (floor_physics: pharma-style plant, tanks drained and refilled, 60 g/L). PIVOTAL: with the medium price, the top driver of R.

inputs.name: aa_intensity
inputs.source: [GFI Dec 2025, read in full; research_notes/nutrient_floor.md; chosen 2026-11-19] amino acids a kilo of wet cells takes up, at the floor: GFI's most efficient of eight estimates (200-650 g; 350 g is the middle). Humbird's stoichiometry (Reaction 2.11) gives 0.26 kg of pure amino acids (Table 3.4); a kilo of wet cells is about 15-20% protein
inputs.note: stoichiometric -> does NOT scale with media efficiency. Before 2026-11-19: 0.337 kg of soy hydrolysate at $2/kg ($0.67 a kilo). GFI: hydrolysates cannot supply glutamine, arginine, asparagine, cystine or serine, so those come from fermentation at the prices of aa_bulk_price

inputs.name: aa_bulk_price
inputs.source: [GFI Dec 2025, Table 1, read in full] feed-grade amino acids, the unweighted mean of 22 (low food-grade 11.59, high food-grade 23.18); weighted by GFI's own need profiles (Table 2: FSF4 medium $5.74, modified CHO medium $6.47) it is bracketed, so the unweighted mean is kept (research_notes/nutrient_floor.md section 7); Humbird's base case paid $15-16
inputs.note: the floor: what the cells must eat at the cheapest grade GFI prices, in the long run at industry scale. Serine is the largest single cost (30% of FSF4's amino-acid cost) and GFI's $10/kg for it is hypothetical: world output is about 400 t a year and no tonne quote is public. So $6.36 assumes new serine capacity; at today's quotes (serine near $20-30/kg) the floor would be about $2.35-2.45, not $2.00 (research_notes/evidence_amino_acid_prices.md, 2026-11-21). inputs.name: plant_floor
inputs.source: [floor_physics; 13.8 until 2026-11-21, when the building's power began to follow its floor and class] plant cost per kg of real cells if everything that has been costed for animal cells works together, financed like a mature food industry: a food-grade plant without clean rooms ($810k per m3 in 2025 prices) plus a hollow-fibre filter loop to hold cells back (retention.py), 20 m3 tanks in perfusion at the density CO2 removal allows (120 g/L), efficient 3 ng cells, 91% uptime: capital, maintenance and insurance $7.5 + labour $2.6 + utilities $0.7 + consumables $3.0 (of which filter membranes $1.9 and bubble protectant $0.7), per kilo of cells harvested. MOVED 2026-11-20 from $10.8 to $13.8, to what floor_physics.tiers() gives after that day's model batch (the value had been left behind): bubbles kill 8% of the cells grown and 2% are lost at harvest, so every line is per kilo harvested; a tank in perfusion takes twice the fed-batch crew; the filter membrane lasts 2,415 litres a m2; the plant buys more medium-preparation equipment for the litres it passes; utilities are counted in Humbird's four parts. Until 2026-11-15 (late) it was $9.8, with a hoped-for device at $89k per m3 and no protectant
inputs.note: THE FLOOR'S PLANT TERM (2026-11-14). Each element is allowed by physics and claimed or shown somewhere, never together: food-grade 20 m3 tanks run today (Vow); perfusion above 100 g/L is shown at 10 L (SuperMeat, Pasitka); a way to hold cells back at 20 m3 is not shown; efficient cells are not shown; 91% uptime is Humbird's figure, which he calls 'rather aggressive'. FINANCING: the yearly charge is plant_charge_mature (17.3%), because the floor is a long-run case compared with meat, a mature industry; at the first-plant rate (23.6%) this term is $16.5. tests/test_floor_physics.py ties this value to the module

inputs.name: plant_floor_lo
inputs.source: [floor_physics; 8.76 until 2026-11-21 (the building's power by floor and class)] THE FRONTIER: the same case in a plant that costs what microbial fermentation plants cost today ($190k per m3: Liberation Labs, Quorn), at the same financing, buying its oxygen (such plants have no oxygen unit). MOVED 2026-11-20 from $6.3 to $8.76, to what floor_physics.tiers() gives after that day's model batch, for the reasons given under plant_floor (cells killed by bubbles and lost at harvest, twice the crew in perfusion, the membrane's life, medium preparation, utilities in four parts). $4.9 before 2026-11-15 (late): no filter membranes, no protectant, no oxygen
inputs.note: such plants exist, for microbes, with 150 m3 vessels. Nobody has costed or built one for animal cells, whose cultures are far easier to contaminate. $9.5 at the first-plant rate. CROSS-CHECK (research_notes/plant_capital_crosscheck.md): the price holds at small tanks. Humbird's own baker's-yeast plant costs $57k per m3 with 200 m3 fermentors and $130k with 27 x 20 m3 (his Table A.5; about $175k in 2025 prices). And two published designs FOR ANIMAL CELLS assume this level: CE Delft 2021 $167-277k per m3 (food-grade, no clean rooms) and Negulescu 2023 $209k (42 m3 tanks). Humbird's animal-cell plant is 5x his yeast plant at the same tank size: sterile seed train, media handling, oxygen supply, a higher installation factor and clean rooms. Whether animal cells need all of that is the open question

inputs.name: plant_floor_hi
inputs.source: [floor_physics] the cautious case: Humbird's sterile pharma-style plant ($908k per m3), tanks half-drained and refilled with no cell retention, 85% uptime, at his first-plant financing (23.6% a year)

inputs.name: plant_charge_mature
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] the yearly charge on a plant financed like a mature food industry: capital recovery at i = 5.4% over n = 20 years (8.3%) plus his 4% maintenance and 5% insurance
inputs.note: GROUNDING, all from Humbird's report: Sect. 3.1 gives the 2019 cost of capital of the food processing sector as 5.4% (against 8.5% for pharma and biotech, and the 7.5% of Beyond Meat that he adopts); his baker's-yeast benchmark (Appendix A) uses a 20-year plant life, where his cultivated-meat plants use 10 (the benchmark's interest rate is 10%, HIGHER than his 7.5%: it supports the 20 years, not a cheaper rate; its payment is 11.7% a year. Corrected 2026-11-20, research_notes/study_comparison.md). CCF = i / (1 - (1 + i)^-n) = 0.083. Maintenance and insurance are kept at his 4% and 5%, which he also applies to the yeast plant. Used for the floor and the frontier, which are long-run cases set against meat; the default and the cautious cases keep the first-plant rate (humbird_plant_charge). lo: CE Delft 2021's 30-year payback with no return (3.3% + 9%; the study states payback years, 4 or 30, and no interest rate). hi: the first-plant rate

inputs.name: pf_batch_end_x
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived; judgement] how far above the waste level a perfusion tank is held at (the ammonia limit, and the lactate the salt allows) a tank that is not washed out may end its cycle. Its waste builds up with its cells, so only the last doublings see the higher level. Humbird's own fed-batch design (1,849 kg in 16 m3, 116 g/L of his enhanced cells: 0.056 mol ammonia and 0.56 mol lactate a kilo) holds 6.5 mmol/L of ammonia and 65 mmol/L of lactate if all the waste its cells made is counted, 1.3 times the 5 and 50 he holds perfusion to
inputs.note: HOW HUMBIRD COUNTS IT (back-test 2026-11-20, research_notes/humbird_backtest.md): his simulation ends at 5 and 50 by his own count (Sect. 4.1, Fig. 4.2), because it starts each tank from fresh medium and 482 kg of seed cells and counts only the waste the 1,367 kg grown in the production tank make: 120 g/L x 0.739 x 0.0563 = 5.0 mmol/L (Fig. 2.8b); his wild-type cells the same way, 7.1 g/L x 0.75 x 0.952 = 5.0. The seed cells arrive in about 4 m3 of seed culture that ended at the same level, which he leaves out. This model counts all of it (the litres a kilo leaves with hold all the waste it made), so his design sits at 1.3 to 1.35 times the level. humbird_check.py sets this input to 1 / (1 - 482/1,849) = 1.35 and switches the slowdown off to price his design as he counts it. ADDED 2026-11-19 (scenario restructure): litres per kilo must be at least waste made per kilo / level allowed, in any mode, so the density of an unwashed tank is this factor x the level / the waste made per kilo (mmol/L / (mol/kg) = g/L). Before, the cap was Humbird's 120 g/L scaled by the waste, which let the low-lactate example's fed-batch end at 7.8 mmol/L of ammonia against the 4 its perfusion is held to. Evidence, both ways (research_notes/vessels_and_modes.md section 10): ammonia: unadapted meat-relevant cells lose about 10% of growth at 1-3 mM and 50% at 3-10 mM (ammonia_tolerance_and_filter_life.md); CHO fed-batch ends at 5-15 mM. Lactate: CHO fed-batch peaks at 10-94 mM (Freund 2018), harm begins near 20-40 mM in CHO, meat-cell processes hold under 30 mM (Pasitka 2024), myoblasts grow faster at 5 mM. 1.0 holds the batch to the perfusion level; 2.0 lets the last doubling run where growth is about a quarter slower (pf_batch_half_x), a cost the model charges

inputs.name: pf_batch_half_x
inputs.source: [ammonia_tolerance_and_filter_life.md, judgement] the waste level at which growth halves, as a multiple of the level a perfusion tank is held at (where growth loss is small, about 10%). Sets how much slower the last doublings of a batch that ends above that level grow: growth falls as 1 / (1 + (c / K)^h), with h = ln 9 / ln(this), so the loss is 10% at the limit and 50% at this multiple of it
inputs.note: ADDED 2026-11-19. Unadapted meat-relevant cells: 10% loss at about 1-3 mM ammonia and 50% at about 3-10 mM (catfish ovary about 0.6 and 3; 3T3 about 1.5 and 8; HFF-1 about 2 and 10), ratios of 2.5-5. Charged only above the steady-state level, as perfusion is charged nothing at it

inputs.note: the density a 20 m3 tank can hold even when waste is washed out by perfusion. Small tanks are oxygen-limited instead (195 g/L at 2 m3)

inputs.note: lo: Negulescu 2023's designs (12.8-13.5); Humbird: '<~25' with air under cell-culture sparging limits; hi: '<50' for animal cells [pf-tea, engineering.yaml, citing Humbird 2021]. Microbial fermenters reach 150-200, but bursting bubbles kill animal cells

inputs.name: pf_uptime

inputs.source: [assumed] share of the tank drained at each harvest in fill-and-draw

inputs.source: [GOOD Meat, Believer, Wildtype and Vow regulatory filings: bulk cell mass, no maturation] hours the cells spend in the tank at no growth before harvest, to mature muscle or fat (floor_physics.explore's mature_h)
inputs.note: references: 0 for the products near market; 4 days, Meatable 2024 (company claim); 7 days for muscle (Cultivated Meat book; Mattick 2015; Tuomisto 2022); 14 and 28 days for fat. While maturing the cells respire at their upkeep rate and use medium at that rate; a continuous tank holds its harvest in a maturation vessel priced as tank capacity

inputs.name: pf_fedbatch_doublings
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Fig. 4.3: production batch grows 482 -> 1,849 kg (1.9 doublings); seed splits of 2-3 doublings are the recommended range

inputs.note: perfusion with an unspecified retention device at a scale nobody has run; see METHODS 'Reactor type and mode'

inputs.name: pf_capex_no_cleanroom
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] his fed-batch plant with the clean room replaced by a sanitary hall: Table 4.2 prices the cell-culture hall (5,268 m2 on 2 levels) at $39.6M as a Class 8 clean room, $3,760 per m2-level (Table 3.2); at the 'Sanitary' rate of $1,980 it is $20.9M. inputs.name: pf_capex_retention
inputs.source: [Pasitka SI Tables S1 and S4, derived] a hoped-for filter-free device to hold cells back in large tanks: '2 x Large-Scale PD' at $1.21M each for 2 x 25 m3, x 1.84 for engineering, construction, fees and contingency

Added to the capital of the large-tank perfusion cases. hi: Humbird's ATF filters cost $38.5M for 192 m3 before installation, about $460k per m3 of total investment (and $4.6/kg of membranes besides), which is why his perfusion design stops at 2 m3. 2024 prices; not escalated

inputs.name: pf_run_days
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Sect. 4.2: perfusion runs of about 33 days; with his 91% uptime that leaves 3.3 days to clean, restart and regrow
inputs.note: Used by the page's 'build your own case' controls: a run ends at this length or when it is contaminated, whichever comes first. The restart time is derived from pf_uptime (perfusion) and pf_uptime_realistic (drained and refilled), so a run with no losses reproduces those uptimes

inputs.name: pf_hazard_pharma
inputs.source: [research pass, derived] chance per day of losing a run to contamination in large biopharma plants: about 2% of batches (Humbird's report) over runs of about two weeks
inputs.note: REFERENCE POINTS shown beside the lever, not used in the floor (which assumes none): 0.2% a day for biopharma contamination, 0.7% for biopharma losses from all causes (7.6% of batches), and 1-2% a day for cultivated meat today, from a survey in which makers lost 11.2% of batches (19.5% beyond flask scale; Compr. Rev. Food Sci. Food Saf. 2025) if those batches ran 10-20 days, which the survey does not state. See reports/'Continuous harvest bioreactor progress.md'

inputs.name: pf_blend_filler_price
inputs.source: [Pasitka] the plant ingredients blended with cells in its hybrid product, at the price that paper uses
inputs.note: for the page's blend lever only

inputs.name: pf_medium_l_floor
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] the least liquid a kg of cells needs to carry its nutrients in: the medium use of his efficient-cell designs, about a quarter of the 30.5 L/kg a company reports
inputs.note: a lower bound on litres per kg in the page's 'build your own case' controls; the waste the cells make usually needs more (pf_nh3_*, pf_lac_*)

inputs.name: pf_nh3_efficient
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] ammonia made per kg of cells grown by his enhanced cells: Reaction 2.11, 0.004 mol per mol of dry cell mass, x 13.6 mol per kg wet
inputs.note: 13.6 mol/kg = 300 g dry matter per kg wet over 22.06 g/mol for CH1.68 O0.34 N0.21 (his Table 2.1). The 0.004 is rounded: Reaction 2.10 makes one ammonia for ten lactate (his note 67), which with 0.558 mol of lactate gives 0.056. Left at 0.054 (back-test 2026-11-20): lactate sets the litres in his design either way. All of it comes from catabolism, so per kg it scales with the upkeep burned (slower cells make more)

inputs.name: pf_nh3_wild
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] the same for ordinary (wild-type) cells: Reaction 2.9, 0.070 mol per mol of dry cell mass

inputs.name: pf_lac_efficient
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] lactate, enhanced cells: Reaction 2.11, 0.041 mol per mol of dry cell mass

inputs.name: pf_lac_wild
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] lactate, ordinary cells: Reaction 2.9, 0.474 mol per mol of dry cell mass

inputs.name: pf_glc_kg
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] glucose used per kg of cells grown by his enhanced cells: 0.558 mol lactate at his stated lactate:glucose of 0.50
inputs.note: used only when the lactate yield is set explicitly (explore lac_yield). lo-1.0 = 0.4-0.6 kg glucose per kg dry x 0.30 dry/wet (waste_tricks_sizing.md, consistent with CHO at a yield of 1.41); hi = Humbird's wild-type cell (6.4 mol lactate at 1.77). Which applies to a meat cell is unmeasured

inputs.name: pf_glc_anabolic
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, reaction 2.11, derived] glucose built into a kilo of cells (lipid, carbohydrate, nucleotides): 0.065 of his 0.147 mol glucose per C-mol of dry cells, at 13.6 C-mol per kg wet. Protein comes from the amino acids. With all lipid fed it falls by three-quarters
inputs.note: GLUCOSE BALANCE (audit 2026-11-19, glucose check): the scenarios derive glucose per kilo from what the cells build, burn and ferment: G = [anabolic x (1 - 0.75 fat fed) + (O2 - 2.25 NH3)/6] / (1 - Y/2), with Y the lactate yield on total glucose. It reproduces Humbird's enhanced cell (2.0 mol/kg at Y 0.28) and gives 4.8 against his 4.53 for his wild type. The cells measured so far (Y 1.05) need about 4.5 mol/kg, not the 0.84 they were given, which could not supply their own oxygen use.

inputs.name: pf_sorbent_q
inputs.source: [derived, not measured; waste_tricks_sizing.md A2] ammonium a sorbent holds at 3-5 mM against 140 mM sodium
inputs.note: mass-action exchange with selectivities of 0.6-3 for clinoptilolite, zirconium phosphate and cation resin; pure-solution capacities (0.9-5.5) do not apply in medium. No capacity has been measured in medium

inputs.name: pf_sorbent_price
inputs.source: [assumed] a graded, sterilised exchanger fit for medium
inputs.note: bulk natural zeolite is $0.05-0.30/kg (USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, read in full); no price was found for a sterile medium-grade zeolite, resin or zirconium phosphate; 5-20 is an assumption

inputs.name: pf_sorbent_cycles
inputs.source: [assumed] times the sorbent is used before it is thrown away (1 = single use)
inputs.note: no regeneration count in medium was found; 50 is a hope, not a number (waste_tricks_sizing.md)

inputs.name: pf_nh3_limit
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Sect. 2.3: 'consider the limits of 5 mmol/L NH3 and 50 mmol/L lactate'; he cites 2-10 mmol/L reported for mammalian cells
inputs.note: evidence pass 2026-11-16 (research_notes/ammonia_tolerance_and_filter_life.md): unadapted meat-relevant cells (catfish ovary, 3T3, pig muscle stem cells, bovine FAPs) lose 10-55% of growth rate at 2.5-5 mM when spiked; CHO and adapted hybridomas tolerate more. Kept at 5 because the low-lactate example assumes cells that tolerate it and no meat cell has been measured at density; P(within 1.5x of the truth) about 45%, with the risk mostly below

inputs.name: pf_lac_limit
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Sect. 2.3, as above
inputs.note: Humbird's own figure, kept for his design (explore()'s default for `lac_limit`) and drawn in its band since 2026-11-20. The scenarios take sc_lac_limit. lo: the upper end of the textbook range (under 10 to 22 mM, Cultivated Meat, Table 2, citing Hassell 1991)

inputs.name: pf_maintenance_share
inputs.source: [GFI 2025 / Miller 1987, judgement] share of a cell's oxygen uptake at a 24 h doubling time that is upkeep (it runs whether or not the cell grows); the rest rises in proportion to the growth rate
inputs.note: qO2(mu) = qO2(24 h) x [share + (1 - share) x mu / mu(24 h)]. lo=0.31: GFI's 2025 growth-modelling review, Fig. 3.5b, from Wagner et al. 2011 (cells at zero growth took up 12-67% of their exponential-phase oxygen, mean 31%; the fit gives a true yield of 2.9 g dry cells per g O2). Miller et al. 1987 put upkeep at 62% of ATP use in hybridoma at 0.66 per day. hi=1.0: Humbird's assumption (upkeep only). 0.5 sits between the two measurements. At 24 h the uptake is West's law whatever the share, so Humbird's designs are unaffected; it matters for faster and slower cells. The review calls this 'a gap for CM-relevant cell lines'

inputs.name: pf_mix_ratio_20m3
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] oxygen transfer the mixing rule allows in a 20 m3 stirred tank, relative to the oxygen-transfer limit
inputs.note: Humbird's rule (Sect. 2.3, after his ref. 127): mixing time t_m must stay below 1/kLa. His Eq. 2.18 gives t_m = 6 T^(2/3) (P/V rho)^(-1/3) (D/T)^(-1/3) (H_L/T)^2.5 = 141 s at 20 m3 (liquid height 1.6 T from his Fig. 2.5, D = T/3, and 43 W/m3, the power at which the smallest eddies are 20 um: his Eq. 2.17 with 50x peak dissipation and water at 37 C). His Eq. 2.16 gives kLa = 0.075 (P/V)^0.47 u_s^0.8 = 26.4 per hour at 0.006 m/s, so 1/kLa = 137 s. 137/141 = 0.97: the two limits coincide at 20 m3, as his text says. At fixed shape and power t_m grows as V^(2/9), so the mixing-limited density falls as (V / 20)^(-2/9). Hydrostatic pressure, which helps oxygen in tall tanks, is left out. Used by the page's 'build your own case' controls

inputs.name: pf_osm_base
inputs.source: [typical] osmolality of fresh culture medium for mammalian cells

inputs.name: pf_osm_limit
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived; Zhu 2005] the salt strength at which growth is taken to stop: the level that Humbird's own two limits imply together (100 mbar of CO2 and 50 mmol/L of lactate, each with its sodium, in a 300 mOsm medium at pH 7.2 come to 413)
inputs.note: Holding the pH against dissolved CO2 takes bicarbonate, and neutralising lactate takes base; both add salt. CHO cells showed no obvious change at 400-450 mOsm/kg from salt alone and a 20% drop at 400-450 combined with 190-210 mbar of CO2 (Zhu et al. 2005, via research_notes/co2_sparging_settling.md); hybridoma growth fell 63% at 415 with 260 mbar. Across four sources (research_notes/perfusion_rate_osmolality.md) growth starts to fall at about 320-400 mOsm/kg and is halved at about 430-465, so 415 sits where growth is clearly slowed but not stopped: a single limit stands in for a gradual decline. Applied in perfusion only

inputs.name: pf_ph
inputs.source: [typical] the pH the tank is held at (setpoints near 7.0 are common; 6.85-7.8 has been tested)
inputs.note: sets how much bicarbonate a given CO2 level needs: [HCO3-] = dissolved CO2 x 10^(pH - pK1)

inputs.name: pf_pk1
inputs.source: [textbook] apparent first dissociation constant of carbonic acid in medium at 37 C

inputs.name: pf_co2_henry
inputs.source: [textbook] solubility of CO2 in water at 37 C (2.46 mmol/L at 100 mbar)

inputs.name: pf_hco3_base
inputs.source: [derived] bicarbonate already in fresh medium: equilibrium with 50 mbar of CO2 at pH 7.4, the usual incubator condition; only bicarbonate above this adds to the salt strength

inputs.name: pf_min_perfusion
inputs.unit: mL per g wet cells per day
inputs.source: [judgement within a measured range] the least medium flow a cell needs for everything other than ammonia and lactate: other by-products that build up, and nutrients that run out
inputs.note: The bioprocess measure is the cell-specific perfusion rate. Measured for CHO cells (research_notes/perfusion_rate_osmolality.md): 50 pL per cell per day sustained 2.1 x 10^8 cells per mL with more giving no benefit (Clincke et al. 2013, full text); 14-30 sustained 2.2-2.4 x 10^8 at slow growth and 8-10 only held the culture without growth (Mayrhofer et al. 2020); unoptimised processes run at 50-300. For a 17 um cell (2.7 ng) 10 / 25 / 50 pL is 3.7 / 9.3 / 18.5 mL per gram per day; cell size was not reported for the low figures, so they could be up to 1.8 times higher. The default 7.5 is the value at which this stops binding for the floor's efficient cells (10.8 L/kg at a 24 h doubling time, against 11.2 from lactate), so the floor assumes cells better than typical pharma practice (9.3) and within what has been reached. Litres per kg = this / growth rate per day, so slow cells need more. One company's chicken process (30.5 L/kg at half a doubling a day) works out to 10.6

inputs.name: pf_cell_density
inputs.source: [calibrated; research_notes/co2_sparging_settling.md] density of an animal cell, set so that a 14 um CHO cell settles at its measured 1.45 cm/h
inputs.note: measured single-cell settling: CHO 1.45 cm/h, hybridoma 2.9; working settlers are sized at 0.7-1.0

inputs.name: pf_medium_density
inputs.source: [typical] density of culture medium at 37 C

inputs.name: pf_medium_viscosity
inputs.source: [typical] viscosity of culture medium at 37 C (water is 0.69)

inputs.name: pf_plate_gap
inputs.source: [typical] spacing of the plates of an inclined (lamella) settler; they stand at 60 degrees

inputs.name: pf_anoxia_min
inputs.source: [research_notes/co2_sparging_settling.md] time cells spend in working inclined settlers (60-90 minutes), taken as what they tolerate without oxygen
inputs.note: at 120 g/L the cells use up the dissolved oxygen in seconds, so the whole stay in a settler is without oxygen unless the settler is cooled

inputs.name: pf_clump_packing
inputs.source: [assumed] share of a clump's volume that is cells (random packing)

inputs.name: pf_pco2_limit
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Sect. 2.3: dissolved CO2 kept below a partial pressure of 100 mbar ('productivity is maximized when pCO2 is maintained in' a range below it)
inputs.note: The level animal cells tolerate while GROWING. Evidence (research_notes/co2_sparging_settling.md): CHO lost 9% of its growth rate at 150 mmHg (200 mbar) with osmolality controlled (Zhu 2005) and about half near 260 mbar with osmolality raised; a defensible range is 100 / 160 / 200 mbar. CHO and hybridoma only: nothing is published for muscle, fibroblast or fish cells

inputs.name: pf_gas_velocity
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Sect. 2.3: 'Sparging is limited to a superficial velocity of 0.006 m/s at the top of the vessel' (0.1 vvm in a 20 m3 tank); his recasting of guidance that the maximum sparge rate 'is usually <0.1 vvm' (he cites Ozturk 1996 and Poertner 2015, neither readable by us)
inputs.note: NOT A MEASURED LIMIT (research_notes/gas_flow_cap.md). A 1990s rule of thumb, reportedly for 'cell lysis and foaming', turned into a velocity for one tank. Nienow 2006 (read in full): large tanks use 0.1-2 mm/s and the upper limit with protectant 'is not established'. What we found: (1) damage from bursting bubbles scales with gas per litre (vvm), as CO2 removal does, so it does not worsen with tank size; with 2 g/L poloxamer and drilled-hole spargers 0.2 vvm did no harm at 60-80 million cells/mL up to 200 L (abstract), without protectant 0.1 vvm kills cells ten times faster than they grow; (2) foam scales with velocity, is unmeasured against it, and is the likeliest cap; (3) no published culture at 6 mm/s at any scale, and none above 200 L combines 50 million cells/mL with 0.05 vvm; tanks of 1-25 m3 are reported at 0.002-0.02 vvm. Defensible range 2 / 5 / 9 mm/s; the model's rough judgement (made while building the model with an AI assistant, for the reasons above) that 6 mm/s is usable at 20 m3 and 120 g/L is about 45%. Humbird's optimistic design keeps 6 because it takes the favourable end of each range. The exhaust gas leaves tall tanks close to saturated with CO2 (four sources), which is what the balance assumes. Vendors and the published CO2 scale-up rule state the limit in vvm (0.1, up to 0.2 in enhanced single-use designs, to 2 m3); foam, the likeliest real cap, scales with velocity, so the cap stays a velocity. A vvm reading would let a taller tank take more gas (research_notes/evidence_gas_flow_units.md)

inputs.name: pf_aspect
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Fig. 2.5: a tank built twice as tall as wide, filled to 80%, so the liquid is 1.6 times as deep as the tank is wide

inputs.name: pf_rq
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] Reaction 2.11: 0.455 mol CO2 made per 0.378 mol O2 used

inputs.name: pf_rq_lipid
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] CO2 released by making the cells' lipid from glucose, per oxygen used: Reaction 2.2 (0.049 glucose -> 0.205 lipid + 0.090 CO2 per mol of dry cell mass, no oxygen) over Reaction 2.11's 0.378 mol O2. Feeding all the lipid takes RQ from 1.204 to 0.966
inputs.note: Carbon and electron balance check: lipid (CH2 O0.13) carries 1.74 more electrons per carbon than glucose; 0.205 C-mol x 1.74 / 4 = 0.089 mol CO2. Humbird's lipid is 15% of dry mass (Table 2.1)

inputs.name: pf_fat_kg
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] lipid in a kg of wet cells: 15% of the 300 g of dry mass (Table 2.1)

inputs.name: pf_fat_price
inputs.source: [assumed] fatty acids fed to the culture, at about a vegetable-oil price
inputs.note: the oil itself is cheap; delivering it to cells in serum-free medium needs a carrier (albumin, cyclodextrin) or an emulsion, which is not priced here; hi stands for a chemically defined concentrate

inputs.name: ge_atp_per_o2
inputs.source: [textbook] oxidative phosphorylation at a P/O ratio of about 2.5

inputs.name: pf_protectant_dose
inputs.source: [gas_flow_cap.md] poloxamer 188 in the medium: the dose with which dense pharma cultures took 0.1-0.2 vvm without extra cell death, which the model's 6 mm/s relies on
inputs.note: Humbird recommends more than 0.5 g/L for vigorously sparged cultures (Sect. 2.3); dense high-gas runs used 2-5 g/L (research_notes/gas_flow_cap.md). It passes the filter and leaves with the medium.

inputs.name: pf_protectant_price
inputs.source: [assumed] poloxamer 188 bought by the tonne: no bulk price found; catalogue prices are $230-260/kg in 10-25 kg packs (Sigma-Aldrich, search summary), tonne-scale excipients sell at a fraction
inputs.note: Since 2026-11-21 (research_notes/evidence_poloxamer_price.md): lo $5 = industrial-grade EO/PO copolymer near commodity surfactant prices (BASF sells one in 600 kg containers); hi $100 = pharma grade by the tonne at about a third of the 25 kg catalogue price (a guess). Before: lo 10, hi 120, about half the small-pack catalogue price. It was the catalogue price itself ($260) until 2026-11-16, when the scenarios' bands began to draw this input; at 260 the draws' median tonne price was $87/kg, above what the catalogue-to-bulk gap of excipients suggests. The catalogue price stays in RESULTS as a what-if. At 2 g/L and $30/kg it is $0.06 a litre of medium: $0.67/kg of cells at 11 L/kg, $1.7 at 28 L/kg. A supplier quote would replace the assumption (TODO.md).

inputs.name: pf_o2_microbial
inputs.source: [model choice, 2026-11-15] 1: the yeast-style plant class buys its oxygen (pi_o2_feed x pi_o2_price), as plants built item by item do; 0: no oxygen cost (earlier versions)

inputs.name: pf_antifoam_otr
inputs.source: [judgement, effect reported] oxygen transfer from the sparger with antifoam present, relative to without: the middle of the reported 0-50% cut
inputs.note: research_notes/gas_flow_cap.md (follow-up 2): antifoams cut kLa by 0 to about 50% depending on type and dose (snippet- and abstract-level sources there). 1 keeps Humbird's oxygen transfer; at 0.5 the oxygen limit of the reference tank falls from 195 to about 97 g/L and binds before CO2. Applied to the sparger only.

inputs.name: pf_co2_strip_eff
inputs.source: [calibrated] how close the exhaust gas comes to equilibrium with the liquid
inputs.note: THE CO2 BALANCE. CO2 leaves a sparged tank only in the exhaust gas. Gas passes at u_s / H_L tank volumes per second (superficial velocity over liquid depth) and can carry at most pCO2 / RT of CO2, so the most the tank can remove is (u_s / H_L) x pCO2 / RT. The cells make RQ x qO2 per gram. With Humbird's limits that gives 125 g/L at 20 m3 and 58 g/L at 200 m3, against his 120-150 and 70 (Fig. 2.8b): the balance reproduces his curve, and its (V)^(-1/3) fall with size is geometry (liquid depth). This factor, 0.96, sets the 20 m3 value to the 120 g/L the floor uses (pf_x_co2_20m3). Perfusion does not help: at 11 L/kg the liquid carries off about 4% of the CO2

inputs.name: pf_o2_purity
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Sect. 2.3: the tanks are sparged with 90% O2 made on site by vacuum pressure-swing adsorption (VPSA)

inputs.name: pf_back_pressure
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Sect. 4.1: '1.33 bar (5 psig) back pressure at the top'; his gas velocity limit is defined at the top of the vessel

inputs.name: pf_o2_price
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Sect. 2.3: on-site VPSA oxygen at 'a size-dependent effective cost of $0.10-0.20/kg O2' (2018 prices; escalated with running costs)
inputs.note: hi: Humbird's own plant tables imply more. His Table 4.1 lists a 25,000 t/y VPSA at $8.84M bare for 480 m3 of tanks (about 13% of direct plant cost once installed), which at his 23.6% yearly charge plus Table 4.4's power is about $0.25-0.33 per kg O2 [derived]. The oxygen plant is sized by the gas flow, not by what the cells use: his design feeds about 3.7 kg O2 per kg of cells (25,000 t/y for 6,800 t/y of cells) and the cells use 0.2, so about 95% is vented

inputs.name: ge_d_co2
inputs.source: [textbook, scaled] diffusivity of CO2 in water: 1.92e-9 at 25 C, scaled to 37 C by temperature over viscosity (x1.34)
inputs.note: not corrected for the cells in the way; +-20%

inputs.name: ge_d_o2
inputs.source: [textbook, scaled] diffusivity of O2 in water: 2.1e-9 at 25 C, scaled as above

inputs.name: ge_o2_henry
inputs.source: [textbook] solubility of O2 in culture medium at 37 C: about 1.0 mmol/L against pure oxygen at 1 bar (water is 1.05), 0.2 against air

inputs.name: ge_do_setpoint
inputs.source: [typical] dissolved oxygen a culture is held at, about a quarter of saturation with air

inputs.name: ge_o2_bar
inputs.source: [assumed] pressure of pure oxygen inside the fibres
inputs.note: a dense (non-porous) wall can hold more than 1 bar without bubbling; the liquid then returns to the tank far above air saturation, which may harm cells

inputs.name: ge_buffer
inputs.source: [assumed] buffering of the culture other than bicarbonate
inputs.note: Bicarbonate can only turn into CO2 if something supplies the acid. Blood has haemoglobin (about 30 mmol/L per pH); fresh medium has about 0.5 (1 mmol/L phosphate). The cells' own contents might add 3-6 at 12-18% of the volume, if CO2 crossing their membranes brings it into play within seconds [inference, not measured]. In phosphate-buffered saline, carbonic anhydrase on the fibres doubled CO2 removal (Kimmel 2013, Arazawa 2015, read in full); in medium with no buffer it would do little

inputs.name: ge_buffer_medium
inputs.source: [textbook arithmetic] buffer of 1 mmol/L phosphate (DMEM/F12 level, memory) at pH 7.2 with pK 6.8: 2.303 x 1 x 0.715 x 0.285
inputs.note: HEPES (pK about 7.3, 10-25 mmol/L in lab media) would add 6-14, but is 'no longer essential' at large scale and adds salt (patent snippets)

inputs.name: pf_util_time
inputs.unit: $k per m3 of tank a year
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, Table 4.4, derived] power for the building (clean-room air and lighting): $543 per batch of a 20 m3 tank, 150 batches a year (3,600 batches in 24 tanks)
inputs.note: UTILITIES IN FOUR PARTS (back-test against Humbird's Table 4.7, 2026-11-20, research_notes/humbird_backtest.md). explore() charged his $0.94 a kilo to every case, whatever the tank made. His own table is mostly per batch and per year, not per kilo: of $1,700 a batch, $543 is building power (by the year), $773 is water and steam to clean and sterilise the tank (by the run), $326 is the water the medium is made with (by the litre) and $123 is power for oxygen, stirring, cooling and dewatering (by the kilo). His wild-type column shows it: the same plant making 6% as much pays $14.52 a kilo for utilities (Table 4.7), which these four parts give ($14.5) and a flat $0.94 does not. At his fed-batch output (14.2 t per m3 a year, 8.65 L a kilo) the parts sum to $0.94. Since 2026-11-21 this part is times floor_physics.building_power (the buildings' floor at the tank size and the load of each building's class), so his perfusion plant of 2 m3 tanks pays 3.4 times it per m3 (his 3.2). Still not closed there: its water use (26.5 L a kilo) is more than its medium and cleaning account for ($0.72 against his $0.98)

inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived; waste_tricks_sizing.md] ammonia made by cells that make almost no ammonia: his enhanced cell, 0.054, rounded; seen only in engineered (glutamine-synthetase) CHO
inputs.note: GENETIC ENGINEERING. The CHO plateau rate that clears this (0.54 fmol/cell/h) is an upper bound from cells that were not net-growing; nothing at a 24 h doubling

inputs.name: sc_nh3_selected
inputs.source: [Hubalek et al. 2023, full text; waste_tricks_sizing.md] ammonia made by bovine fibro-adipogenic cells when glutamine is replaced by alpha-ketoglutarate, pyruvate or glutamate: 'more than 5-fold' below the 0.70 with glutamine, so under 0.14
inputs.note: FEED CHANGE, then SELECTION. Measured once, in one cell type, in spinner flasks; the same paper's shaker value for ordinary cells is ten times lower than its spinner value, cause unexplained. RANGE WIDENED 2026-11-19 (lo 0.07 -> 0.04; mode and hi kept), after a two-sided pass (ammonia_tolerance_and_filter_life.md, section 10). Lower: the shaker runs found the replacement substrates made no ammonia; other lines on pyruvate released none; CHO adapted to glutamine-free medium by selection grow on glutamate and aspartate with ammonia 'greatly decreased', and the cells' own glutamine synthetase can take ammonia up; so meat cells plausibly reach the lower setting's 0.055 (about 20%), and the ranges overlap. Higher or kept: 0.14 is the one measurement in a stirred vessel of growing cells, an upper bound on a mean of five donors; adaptation slows growth (US 9714293) and slower cells burn more amino acids per kilo; FAPs, not muscle cells; the knock-outs that remove ammonia entirely (ISCCM11 2025 poster: glutaminases and asparaginase) are engineering. So the mode stays at the measurement

inputs.name: mr_ed_nh3

inputs.name: mr_ed_cost_l
inputs.source: [my arithmetic, not a quote] electrodialysis of cell-free permeate: electricity, ion-exchange membranes and the salt it strips with the waste
inputs.note: a litre at the limits holds about 0.03 mol of ammonium and lactate against 0.28 mol of other ions, so without selective membranes 5-20% of the current does the job: 0.15-0.6 mol of charge a litre, 0.006-0.024 kWh at 1.5 V ($0.001-0.002), 0.04-0.16 m2.h of membrane at 100 A/m2 ($0.0005-0.005 at $200/m2 over 1-2 years), and $0.002-0.007 of salt put back. inputs.name: mr_exchange_clearance
inputs.source: [Fresenius Medical Care, FX high-flux dialyser table, in vitro (ISO 8637, QD 500 mL/min), checked 2026-11-21; the FX CorAL 80 510(k) summary K220721 gives 277] small solutes a haemodialyser clears by diffusion, as litres of fluid fully cleared per m2 an hour: the FX 80 clears 278 mL/min of urea at a blood flow of 300 mL/min over 1.8 m2 of fibre (BMC Nephrology 2015, Table 1), 9.3 L/m2/h, rounded to 10
inputs.note: measured on blood (30-40% cells) over 4-hour sessions, not on a meat-cell culture over weeks; against the 5 L/m2/h (rt_flux_lmh) a cell filter passes. At 300 mL/min the clearance is held by the blood flow (278 of 300): with more flow through the fibres it would be higher, so the figure is not generous for a short run; the open question is how it holds over weeks of fouling

inputs.name: sc_wide_bands

inputs.name: sc_nh3_limit
inputs.source: [research_notes/ammonia_tolerance_and_filter_life.md, judgement] ammonia the scenarios' cells tolerate in the tank with little loss of growth. The evidence note's median for meat cells is 3.5-4 mM (80% interval 2-8): unadapted meat-relevant cells lose 10% of growth at about 1-3 mM, meat-cell processes hold 2-3 mM, and some other animal cell lines grow at more (hybridomas at 10-21 mM)
inputs.note: Set 2026-11-19 (audit): every scenario took Humbird's 5 mM (pf_nh3_limit), above the note's own median. Humbird's optimistic design keeps his 5. Drawn in every scenario's band.

inputs.name: sc_lac_limit
inputs.source: [Cultivated Meat (book), Table 2, citing Hassell 1991; Pasitka 2024; Humbird 2021, judgement] lactate the scenarios' cells tolerate in the tank with little loss of growth. The book gives under 10 to 22 mM; Pasitka 2024 held 30 mM in a running culture; Humbird 2021 takes 50
inputs.note: Set 2026-11-20 (research_notes/full_review_2026-11-19.md, section 2, item 1): every scenario took Humbird's 50 mM (pf_lac_limit), which had no range, so no band drew it. Passed by scenarios.always() as `lac_limit`, as sc_nh3_limit is. Humbird's optimistic design keeps his 50. Drawn in every scenario's band.

inputs.name: sc_do_setpoint
inputs.source: [gas_exchange_study.md 10.2; pharma practice, snippet-level sources] dissolved oxygen the scenarios hold the tank at: about 47% of air saturation (air at 37 C: 0.21 mmol/L)
inputs.note: Humbird's oxygen transfer (29 mmol/L/h at kLa 26.4 per hour, 90% oxygen) implies his tank is held at 0.28 mmol/L, 130% of air saturation. Pharma holds 30-50%; cells grow unimpaired at roughly 10-100%, and 200% slowed CHO (gas_exchange_study.md). A lower setpoint widens the driving force for oxygen and needs nothing new. Applied to every scenario since 2026-11-16 (design_space.py found it unused); Humbird's optimistic design keeps his 0.28.

inputs.name: sc_do_scenarios
inputs.source: [model choice, 2026-11-16] 1: the scenarios hold dissolved oxygen at sc_do_setpoint; 0: at the level Humbird's tank implies (earlier versions, and the side studies' snapshots)

inputs.name: sc_restart_neighbour
inputs.source: [arithmetic, judgement] a lost tank reseeded with half the culture of a healthy neighbouring tank, in place of a new seed train: about 2 days to empty, clean and steam the tank, about 1 doubling to regrow both tanks to working density, and the neighbour's lost output counted as about 1 more day of the lost tank's time
inputs.note: The question (2026-11-16): why 14 days and not 1? Regrowing from a seed at about 1 g/L to 120 g/L is about 7 doublings, 7-10 days at 24-36 h, plus cleaning and checks; a neighbour's dense culture skips most of that. The risk is a donor carrying a contaminant not yet detected (a fast contaminant shows on oxygen readings only after 17-51 h, cheap_plant_study.md), so the donor must test clean first. Needs several tanks running; nobody has reported doing it with animal cells at scale.

The earlier value, 3,960 (5 L/m2/h for a 33-day run, from a research pass), gave $0.37. lo: fouled in about 4.5 days at 8.3 L/m2/h (Veje 2024); hi: one TFF hollow fibre lasted 30 days at 7.6 (Clincke 2013). Membranes, not hardware, set the cost of filtering a thick, fast-fed culture. Evidence pass 2026-11-16 (research_notes/ammonia_tolerance_and_filter_life.md): small-pore fibres in dense CHO perfusion foul in about 6-30 days, about 180-2,500 L/m2, and industry designs for 1,000 (median about 1,500). Read with rt_membrane_price: a membrane adds price / life per litre, so 1,500 L/m2 costs nothing extra at $900/m2 or less (filter_flux.break_even_price). Pasitka 2024's Table S6 (600 ATF membranes a year on 50 ATF-10s, one change a month) implies 3,640-9,240 L/m2, the only meat-cell figure and in the upper half of the range, but it is a company's cost assumption, not a measurement (research_notes/evidence_ammonia_and_filter_life.md)
