inputs.name: elasticity_anchor_price
inputs.source: [calibration] the retail price at which the own-price elasticity target (eps_own x cult_sub_mult = -3.6) is imposed when the price coefficient beta is solved
inputs.note: A CALIBRATION DEVICE, NOT A COST. What it pins down is how sharply shoppers respond to price. The evidence for that is at EQUAL price: Van Loo, Caputo & Lusk (2020) put cultivated meat's own-price elasticity there between -0.84 and -3.4, and with this anchor the model gives -1.54 at first contact (golden-guarded, test_golden.py). So the anchor is to be read as 'the price coefficient that puts the at-parity elasticity at -1.54', which no cost input changes. HISTORY: it used to be derived from the cost defaults (it was cultivated's retail price when the demand side was first calibrated), so every cost correction silently re-solved beta; it has been fixed since 2026-11-14. Changing it re-solves beta and every calibrated weight; the kappa range (3-9) is how the model carries the width of the measured bracket

inputs.name: eps_own
inputs.source: [scanner] own-price elasticity of meat demand. Andreyeva, Long & Brownell 2010 (AJPH 100:216) meta-analysis: beef -0.75, pork -0.72, poultry -0.68; Gallet 2010/2012 meta-analysis: -0.7..-1.0 by species/region; plant-based scanner data sits in the same -0.5..-1.4 envelope. -0.9 is the mid-range central.
inputs.note: ONE factor of cultivated's own-price-elasticity TARGET eps_x = eps_own*cult_sub_mult; the shared logit coefficient beta is DERIVED to hit that target at cultivated's own modeled price & share (market_share._derive_beta), so beta moves automatically when this moves. Premium tiers are made LESS elastic in meat_market (cuts x0.8, luxury x0.3): premium buyers are less price-sensitive (Lusk & Tonsor 2016: demand more inelastic at high price).

inputs.name: kappa_base
inputs.source: [structural] how many times more own-price-elastic a single meat PRODUCT is than meat as a category; sets the price weight beta that every product shares
inputs.note: ADDED 2026-11-14 when kappa was split in two. Until then one number, cult_sub_mult, set the shared price weight beta, so raising it made shoppers more sensitive to EVERY price (beans and plant-based included) and the calibration strained (at 9 a solved weight fell to zero). Now kappa_base sets beta (unchanged at 4: a product's own-price elasticity is typically 3-5x its category's), and cult_sub_mult / kappa_base multiplies only cultivated's price DIFFERENCE from the conventional meat beside it. At cult_sub_mult = kappa_base the model is exactly the published one

inputs.name: liking_sd
inputs.source: [fitted, liking_spread.families] spread (standard deviation) across shoppers of liking for cultivated meat, in the model's utils. Fitted with liking_tail, jointly, to the one random-parameter choice experiment on cultivated meat (Van Loo, Caputo & Lusk 2020: its own-price elasticity at four prices, miss 0.02 against 2.56 with every shopper alike), to the share sixteen premium real meats hold at 2, 3 and 4 times the ordinary price, and to farmed salmon's response to its falling price, with the price-insensitive shoppers in the model (since 2026-11-22). The experiment itself estimated 3.6-4.6 on its scale, about 3.3-4.7 utils here.
inputs.note: Not drawn in the bands: equal_price_share is set given it. 0 gives the model as it was before 2026-11-18. lo-hi: about the values whose joint misfit is within 20% of the best at liking_tail = 7 (3.45-3.65) and across tails with liking_tail re-fitted (3.25-4.0, liking_spread.profile). CHANGED 2026-11-22 (fifth batch) from 3.9 with a tail of 4, refitted with the price-insensitive shoppers (price_insensitive_share): they hold buyers far above meat's price, so a narrower spread with a lighter tail fits better (joint misfit 0.87, was 4.20). CHANGED 2026-11-19 from 5.0 with a normal spread: that fit (miss 0.15, elasticity -1.53) rested on fifteen integration points; integrated properly a normal spread of 5 missed by 0.29 with an elasticity of -1.34. With LIKING_FAMILY = 'normal', liking_sd = 5.0 and no price-insensitive shoppers the model of 2026-11-18 is reproduced exactly.

inputs.name: liking_tail
inputs.source: [fitted, liking_spread.families] how heavy the tails of the spread of liking are: the degrees of freedom of a Student's t. The smaller, the more shoppers who like (or dislike) cultivated meat far more than the typical spread, so the more who still buy at three or four times meat's price; at 30 or more it is a normal spread. With liking_sd it is fitted jointly to the choice experiment, the premium real meats and farmed salmon (see liking_sd).
inputs.note: Must be above 2 (below, the spread has no standard deviation). Not drawn in the bands. LOOSELY PINNED: the joint misfit is least at 7 (0.87) and within 20% of the least from 5 to 12 (liking_spread.profile). CHANGED 2026-11-22 (fifth batch) from 4: with the price-insensitive shoppers in the model, the buyers left far above meat's price are partly theirs, and a lighter tail fits better. The three things the misfit does not count, which chose 4 over 3 on 2026-11-19, point the same way: a lighter tail gives a first-contact share nearer the measured (3.8% of all choices at 7, measured 4%), fewer buyers at ten or more times meat's price, and a higher best case. Used only when LIKING_FAMILY is 'student' (for 'mixture' it is the minority's spread as a multiple of the others').

inputs.name: equal_price_share
inputs.source: [judgement, research_notes/liking_spread.md] once cultivated meat is familiar and costs the same as conventional meat, the share of all shoppers' choices (meat, cultivated meat, plant-based meat or no meat) that go to it, at neutral settings (tastes as good, seen as real meat, no health or slaughter-free credit); 14.5% of those who buy a meat. It is first contact plus the model's own fading of novelty (2.8 utils). With the Student's t spread and the price-insensitive shoppers (2026-11-22), 13% in the long run implies 3.8% of all choices at first contact, 4.3% of those who buy a meat: the experiment (Van Loo, Caputo & Lusk 2020) measured 4% and 5%.
inputs.note: THE MODEL'S LARGEST UNKNOWN. Drawn in the bands from a lognormal whose median is the model's own 13%, so half the draws are below the point value and half above. 0.03 and 0.49 are its 5th and 95th percentiles in the sense that they set its spread (sigma = ln(0.49/0.03) / 3.29 = 0.85); because 13% is a little above their geometric mean (12%), the percentiles of the draws themselves are 3.2% and 53% (10th and 90th: 4.4% and 39%). Draws are clipped to 0.5%-80%. 0.49: shoppers end up indifferent on average, the model's implicit premise before 2026-11-18. The literature review (research_notes/what_drives_choice.md) puts the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles at 2%, 10% and 35%. CHANGED 2026-11-19 (audit D1) from a triangular 0.05-0.13-0.49, whose median was 21%, well above the point value it was meant to surround. KEPT AT 13% when the spread became a Student's t (2026-11-19): holding first contact at 5% of ALL choices would give 15%, but 5% is the experiment's share of meat buyers; its share of all choices is 4%, and 13% reproduces both.

inputs.name: best_equal_price_share
inputs.source: [the model's rough judgement, 2026-11-19] the same share in the all-favourable example: once familiar and at equal price, shoppers slightly favour cultivated meat. The all-favourable example takes the favourable end of every uncertain input, and demand is one of them. Its competitor is factory-farmed meat, whose own image (slaughter, antibiotics, disease) none of the precedents for distrusted foods had to face (irradiated food, margarine, modified crops, all against a natural product), and decades of familiarity and a new generation of shoppers are part of it.
inputs.note: Used only by the all-favourable example (scenarios.SCENARIOS['best'].equal_price_share); drawn in its band from 35% to 70%. Every other scenario uses equal_price_share.

inputs.name: cult_sub_mult
inputs.source: [data-bracketed] kappa: HOW MANY TIMES more own-price-elastic CULTIVATED meat is than meat as a CATEGORY. Plain meaning: a 1% rise in cultivated's price loses kappa x 0.9% of its buyers, versus 0.9% for meat-in-general. WHY > 1: the measured -0.9 is the elasticity of the meat CATEGORY, which is inelastic precisely because the category has no close substitute; but a single cultivated product DOES have a near-perfect substitute right next to it (conventional meat, the SAME tissue), so its OWN price matters far more -- a price cut wins buyers fast, a price rise loses them to conventional. kappa therefore sets HOW STEEPLY cultivated's share falls as it gets pricier than conventional (above parity); it does NOT change the at-parity share (where prices are equal).
inputs.note: DEFAULT 4 -> 8.5, 2026-11-14, on two kinds of evidence. (1) Six premium animal products with matched price premiums and volume shares (market_share.ANALOGUES: organic milk, cage-free, organic and omega-3 eggs, organic chicken, all organic meat) take 2-7% of volume at 1.5-2.2x the conventional price. The model's share for a product equal to conventional on everything but price misses them by a typical factor of six at kappa = 4 (log error 1.84), by 2.6 at 8.5 (0.97), and fits best at 10 (0.92). (2) The one choice experiment on cultivated meat (Lusk, below) brackets the at-parity elasticity at [-3.4, -0.84]; kappa = 8.5 gives -3.27 and 9 gives -3.46, just outside. So 8.5 is the best analogue fit that the experiment allows. Range 4 (the old default) to 11. THIS BECAME POSSIBLE when kappa was split (kappa_base): it now multiplies only cultivated's price difference from conventional, so the at-parity share, the plant-based calibration and every other dial are unchanged by it (the solved weights are those of the published model). EARLIER NOTE (2026-11-13, hi 6 -> 9): the organic-chicken check (market_share.organic_premium_check) shows the model gives a real-meat product at a premium far more share than organic chicken's ~2.4%; a higher kappa is the in-model direction of that evidence, so the band now reaches kappa=9, where the implied at-parity elasticity (about -3.2) is still inside the Lusk bracket. The mode stays 4. DATA ANCHOR (the one direct measurement): Van Loo, Caputo & Lusk 2020 (Food Policy 95:101931) priced lab-grown across SIX levels ($2.99-$10.49/lb) in a US choice experiment, identifying its OWN-PRICE ELASTICITY AT PARITY. Their two models bracket it: the conditional logit (price coeff -0.178/$) implies eps_lab ~ -0.84 at $5/lb; the random-parameter logit (mean -0.72/$, with a lab random-coeff SD ~3-4.6 LARGER than its mean -> ~half the population positive, half negative) implies eps_lab ~ -3.4. So the data bracket is eps_lab(at parity, cold) in [-3.4, -0.84]. kappa is the flat-logit STAND-IN for exactly that real_tissue heterogeneity (= a nested-logit dissimilarity parameter), so this is the moment that grounds it: at the central kappa=4 the model's implied at-parity cold elasticity is -1.5, INSIDE the bracket (self-check [4b]; golden-guarded at -1.53827). CORROBORATION: a single product's own-price elasticity is typically ~3-5x its category's (the standard brand-vs-category gap), and cultivated is a closer substitute (same tissue) -> the upper half is apt. RANGE 3-6 spans the bracket's interior (note kappa=3 dips just under the MNL -0.84 end; the floor could tighten to ~3.5, kept at 3 as a mild dovish margin). RESIDUAL CAVEAT (functional form, not fixable by kappa): Lusk measures the elasticity AT PARITY, but the realized headline target eps_x = eps_own*kappa = -0.9*4 = -3.6 is at cultivated's OPERATING POINT R~2.4, where the BLP+kink elasticity is steeper -- matching the at-parity bracket grounds the SHAPE near parity, but the -3.6 at R~2.4 is an EXTRAPOLATION (no DCE has priced cultivated at ~2.4x conventional). The OTHER factor of eps_x, so it moves the DERIVED beta directly; swept lo-hi in self-check [6].

inputs.name: loss_aversion
inputs.source: REFERENCE-DEPENDENT price asymmetry lambda (OFF by default). Consumers may compare each product to the conventional price and feel a premium as a 'loss': a DISCOUNT (below conventional) rewarded at the UNIT rate (+1), a PREMIUM penalised at -lambda, so V_loss_j = -lambda*max(0, price_ratio_j - 1) + 1*max(0, 1 - price_ratio_j). lambda=1 (the DEFAULT) is SYMMETRIC -- the term collapses to a smooth linear (1 - price_ratio) with NO kink, i.e. no loss aversion; lambda>1 adds an asymmetric premium penalty (Tversky-Kahneman 1992 put the loss/gain ratio ~2.25). Applied uniformly to every product (plant-based at 1.77x and cultivated at R), never a cultivated-only cliff.
inputs.note: WHY DEFAULT 1.0 (symmetric, no kink) rather than the TK 2.25: (1) it is NEAR-INERT on the headline anyway -- the beta-derivation absorbs lambda's price slope, so lambda only reshapes the parity KINK, not the elasticity level at the US anchor (lambda 1->2.25 moves the at-parity share <2pp). It does NOT leave the regional roll-up unchanged (corrected 2026-11-13): absorbing lambda pushes beta positive (+0.051 at 2.25), which reverses the income channel so poorer shoppers become LESS price-sensitive; the world share rises from 2.5% to 6.3% and Nigeria's from 0.09% to 1.4%. Regional results at lambda above ~1.65 (where beta crosses zero) are therefore not meaningful. RANGE CAPPED AT 2.25 (the TK median) for a principled reason: the beta-derivation absorbs lambda's price slope only up to lambda~2.6, where beta saturates at its monotonicity cap (beta_cap = 1/p_conv - 1e-3); beyond that the realised own-price elasticity would drift off the eps_own*kappa target (e.g. ~-7 at lambda=4) -- a broken microfoundation, not a meaningful scenario -- so the slider/prior stops at the literature anchor, where the 'only reshapes the kink, not the level' property still holds. (A subtler point: the BLP sub-term's coefficient flips sign around lambda~1.65; above that the price response is carried by the kink rather than the income log, though the HEADLINE elasticity stays on target throughout the capped range.) (2) Bell & Lattin 2000 (Marketing Sci 19:185) show estimated loss aversion in aggregate choice data is largely CONFOUNDED by unmodeled price-response heterogeneity -- and this model already carries that heterogeneity in kappa (cult_sub_mult, the real_tissue random-coefficient stand-in), so a separate asymmetric kink risks DOUBLE-COUNTING it; (3) the model's reference is CONTEXTUAL (the competitor's current price), a cross-sectional comparison that does NOT fade -- distinct from a TEMPORAL reference anchored to a product's own price history, which adapts and is transient (the genuinely time-varying novelty effect lives in the neophobia fade, not here). BONUS: at lambda=1 the model's at-parity own-price elasticity is -0.82, CLOSER to Lusk 2020's measured MNL -0.84 than the kinked lambda=2.25 (-0.50) was. So lambda is now an OFF-by-default exploratory dial (range 1-2.25) for anyone who wants to test reference-dependent asymmetry, not a baked-in behavioral assumption. Its slope still feeds the beta calibration when moved.

inputs.name: w_ratio
inputs.source: [judgement] WEIGHT of the ratio-based price term w_ratio*(-lambda*max(0, R-1) + max(0, 1-R)): the part of the price response that compares each product with the conventional price and carries NO income scaling. The rest of the price response is the BLP income log, which is income-scaled. beta is re-derived for any w_ratio, so the TOTAL own-price elasticity at the US anchor stays on its target (eps_own*kappa) and US results do not move; what w_ratio sets is the SPLIT between the two channels, which decides how much less price-sensitive richer shoppers are than poorer ones, and so the low-income regions and the world roll-up.
inputs.note: No study measures this split for meat; 1.0 (one util per unit of price ratio) is the model's original, previously hard-coded value, kept as the default so published results are unchanged. Range 0.5-1.5 is a judgement band around it. Effect (2026-11-13): world share 1.6% at 0.5, 2.5% at 1.0 and 4.0% at 1.5, with the US everyday share unchanged (8.8%); at 0 (all price response income-scaled) the world share is 1.1%. It is in the tornado (sensitivity.py) rather than the Monte Carlo, because every value needs beta and the calibration re-solved; that tornado is at the US reference income, where its bar is zero by construction, so its effect is the world figure above.

inputs.name: theta_free_M
inputs.source: [NEUTRAL DIAL] MAINSTREAM utility weight on the slaughter-free attribute — THE headline UPSIDE dial. In the rebuilt MNL it is w_slaughter[M], applied to EVERY slaughter-free product (cultivated, plant-based, whole-food). 0 = mainstream indifferent to no-slaughter (cultivated ties conventional at parity); positive = mainstream values cleaner / no-slaughter, so cultivated (and, more weakly, plant-based) gain.
inputs.note: The ethical UPSIDE half of cultivated's standing. ~89% of real PB-meat buyers are non-veg/vegan (GFI 2024) — that flexitarian pull lives HERE (mainstream), not in the 5% ethical core (w_eth). MC prior 0..1: neutral to 'values no-slaughter'.

inputs.name: accept_x
inputs.source: [DIAL] how fully the mainstream credits cultivated's taste / real-meat attribute. In the rebuilt MNL it sets cultivated's taste_quality = (accept_x - 1), weighted by w_taste utils. 1 = tastes as real as conventional (neutral); <1 = a taste deficit.
inputs.note: The taste-FRICTION half of cultivated's standing. In the MNL the utility offset is w_taste*(accept_x-1) utils, weighted by the shared taste coefficient w_taste.

inputs.name: premium_resistance
inputs.source: [assumed] how much less buyers of premium products (wagyu, sushi-grade fish) like a cultivated version, beyond what applies to any cut. It multiplies the premium part of a product's offset only (meat_market.tier_offset): AUTH_PREMIUM_EXTRA (-1.1 utils) times how far the product's price sits between PREMIUM_START (2x) and PREMIUM_FULL (4x) its species' cheapest form. 1 = as set; 0 = a premium product is liked as much as any other cut; 2 = twice the penalty. It does not touch mince, the blend penalty every cut carries (-(1 - cell share) x the real-meat weight), or price sensitivity.
inputs.note: A judgement with no external data: the belief that people buy wagyu or sushi-grade fish partly for the genuine article. Drawn in the bands (0.5-1.5). CHANGED 2026-11-19 (audit D3): until then it also scaled a +0.2 offset for mince, a -0.4 offset for cuts and LOWER price sensitivity for cuts and premium products (x0.8, x0.3), which raised cultivated meat's share wherever it was the dearer product, so more 'resistance' gave a higher share.

inputs.name: real_tissue_x
inputs.source: [IDENTIFYING PREMISE, now a DIAL] whether CULTIVATED meat counts as 'real animal tissue' (1) or not (0). =1 is the model's load-bearing premise: cultivated, being actual cells, INHERITS conventional meat's real-tissue standing and so escapes the plant-based 'not real meat' penalty — the structural reason it can succeed where plant-based stalled. Exposed as a 0/1 dial (default 1) so a SKEPTIC can set it to 0 ('consumers won't credit lab-grown as real meat') and watch cultivated collapse toward the plant-based outcome. Weighted by w_realtissue_M (mainstream) in V_x.
inputs.note: The single most important ASSUMPTION in the model, deliberately made adjustable rather than hardwired. At 1 cultivated > plant-based at parity (the headline ordering); at 0 cultivated becomes a second plant-based product. NOT swept in the MC (it is a scenario axis, like the acceptance dials), but a primary what-if.

inputs.name: real_tissue_p
inputs.source: [product position] whether PLANT-BASED meat counts as 'real animal tissue' (1) or not (0). =0 by definition (plant-based is not animal tissue) — this is the penalty that, with its price premium and taste deficit, keeps plant-based meat at ~1.2%. Exposed for SYMMETRY with real_tissue_x (equal footing): set it to 1 to ask the counterfactual 'what if consumers treated plant-based as equivalent to real meat?' (it would rise sharply). Default 0.
inputs.note: Plant-based gets the SAME machinery as cultivated; the only a-priori difference between the two novel meats is this attribute (and price/taste, which are observed). Equal footing means the asymmetry is a visible DIAL, not a hidden constant.

inputs.name: health_x
inputs.source: [SCENARIO, unidentified] HEALTH-PERCEPTION POSITION of CULTIVATED meat (on the same scale as the other products' health positions, weighted by the segment health weight). POSITIVE = perceived HEALTHIER (a draw: 'clean, no antibiotics, no faecal contamination, controlled fat'); NEGATIVE = perceived LESS healthy ('lab-grown, unnatural, ultra-processed'); 0 = at the conventional reference. Default 0 because the evidence is genuinely TWO-SIDED with no point estimate. A scenario dial like novelty/authenticity: inert at 0 relative to conventional, never re-pins.
inputs.note: Distinct from taste (a_x, sensory) and slaughter-free (theta, ethics). Equal footing with the plant-based health dial. Swept +-0.5 in the MC band.

inputs.name: health_p
inputs.source: [SCENARIO, unidentified] HEALTH-PERCEPTION POSITION of PLANT-BASED meat — the SAME dial as health_x, for equal footing. POSITIVE = the 'plant-based = good for you' health-halo; NEGATIVE = the 'ultra-processed fake meat' backlash. 0 = at the conventional reference. Default 0 and UNIDENTIFIED, like health_x: an exploratory deviation from plant-based's calibrated ~1.2%, not a re-pin.
inputs.note: The term for 'how much of plant-based's plateau is a health-perception problem?'. Swept in MC.

inputs.name: health_w
inputs.source: [position] HEALTH-PERCEPTION POSITION of the WHOLE-FOOD outside option (beans/tofu/lentils): POSITIVE — whole plant foods are widely seen as 'the healthy choice' (dietary guidance ranks legumes above red meat; ~17% name healthfulness the top protein driver, and 'good source of protein' is the #1 healthy-food definer). This positive position, times the SOLVED segment health weight, is what replaces the old free whole-food intercept. Default +2 (a judgement scale set with the weight; only the product depends on data, not the split).

inputs.name: health_c
inputs.source: [position] HEALTH-PERCEPTION POSITION of CONVENTIONAL meat: slightly NEGATIVE — red/processed meat carries a mild 'less healthy' standing (saturated fat, processed-meat guidance) relative to whole plant foods, though it remains a high-quality protein. Small by design; it sets conventional's health standing that the other positions are measured against. Default -0.1, so cultivated (health_x=0, i.e. no antibiotics/contamination, controlled fat) carries a mild +0.1 health edge over conventional — a small, defensible lift to the at-parity share (~47% -> ~49%).

inputs.name: neophobia_p0
inputs.source: [behavioural] plant-based meat's INITIAL (cold-start) novelty attitude — the analogue of neophobia_x0 for cultivated. Plant-based is already MATURE (~1.2%), so its observed position is the calibration target and this cold-start is mostly HISTORICAL / exploratory: it sets where plant-based's own diffusion curve STARTED. Crucially, plant-based's novelty never fully faded into success because it never reached sensory parity (the taste deficit a_p<1 is permanent) — so in the timing chart plant-based is the STALLED counterfactual to cultivated. Default -1.0; fades toward the long-run neophobia_p (default 0) at accept_rate.
inputs.note: Mirrors neophobia_x0 so plant-based has the SAME timing apparatus. PB's stall in the chart is driven by its permanent taste deficit (a_p) + price premium (R_p), not by novelty — novelty fades for both; taste does not. Exploratory (PB is calibrated to its mature share).

inputs.name: price_pb_mult
inputs.source: [GFI] plant-based meat retail PRICE premium vs conventional: GFI/NIQ 2024 put PB meat at +77% per lb (up from +65% in 2022); the gap WIDENED, and 2025 narrowing is an artifact of beef inflation, not PB cost-down
inputs.note: PB meat is a genuine, persistent price PREMIUM — a load-bearing reason its share is small.

inputs.name: price_wf_mult
inputs.source: [BLS] whole-food plant protein staple (dried beans/lentils) $/kg vs commodity meat: US dried beans $3.40/kg (BLS Aug 2025), representative $2-3.5/kg, vs ~$12/kg meat -> ~0.25x. Beans are also ~3-5x cheaper per kg of PROTEIN than beef (VRG 2024).
inputs.note: the outside option is CHEAP; with taste_quality_w and the whole-food HEALTH premium (health_w x the solved segment health weight) it absorbs most ethical demand -> PB stays ~1%.

inputs.name: taste_quality_w
inputs.source: [assumed] whole-food (beans/tofu/lentils) taste/utility AS A MEAT SUBSTITUTE: nutritious and cheap, but quite far from a meat-eating experience. Normalised like (accept_x-1): 0 = as satisfying as real meat, negative = a worse stand-in for meat (-0.7 ≈ a_w 0.3 on the 1=real-meat scale)
inputs.note: NOT load-bearing: the whole-food HEALTH weight (w_health) is SOLVED to hit the meatless / PB-share targets, so it absorbs whatever this taste does not — lowering taste_quality_w just raises the solved health weight, leaving cultivated and plant-based shares unchanged. Set to a plausible 'beans aren't a burger' value; the split between taste and the solved ASC is not identified.

inputs.name: income_ref
inputs.source: [World Bank API, NY.GDP.PCAP.CD] US GDP per head in nominal dollars, 2024 ($86,170; it was the PPP figure $85,810 until 2026-11-20, see meat_market.REGION_INCOME) — the REFERENCE income at which the price coefficient is anchored (so the US/commodity case is unchanged). Only income RATIOS across regions matter, so the absolute level is absorbed by alpha.

inputs.name: income_gradient
inputs.source: [Muhammad/ERS] phi: the DAMPING exponent on the BLP income term. Income enters the price utility as genuine Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes V_price = alpha*ln(y_eff - price_j), with the EFFECTIVE income y_eff = income_ref*(income/income_ref)**phi. phi controls how strongly the BLP curvature is expressed across regions: phi=1 = raw BLP (y_eff = actual income); phi=0 = no income effect (y_eff = income_ref everywhere); 0<phi<1 damps it.
inputs.note: RE-SOLVED 2026-11-20 when incomes became nominal dollars (World Bank 2024: US 86,170, EU 43,314, China 13,293, Brazil 10,311, India 2,592, Nigeria 1,084, world 13,717; the PPP figures were 85,810, 62,266, 27,105, 22,333, 11,159, 6,440, 24,248): phi=0.32 gives a Nigeria/US ratio of cultivated meat's own-price elasticity at equal price of 2.20 (India 1.81, China 1.32), the ~2.2 the note below states. (With PPP incomes, phi=0.5 gave 2.04 at equal price in the current demand model; 0.30 would keep that 2.04.) EARLIER: phi=0.5 gave a Nigeria/US own-price-elasticity ratio ~2.2x (India ~1.8x), matching the empirical food-price-elasticity gradient (poor countries ~2-3x more responsive for meat; Muhammad et al. 2011 USDA ERS, food income-elasticity 0.78 low- vs 0.50 high-income). WHY DAMP: RAW BLP (phi=1) is TOO STEEP for food — it implies a ~6.4x rich->poor elasticity ratio, far above the data; phi damps the EFFECTIVE income inside the log so the BLP curvature matches the empirical gradient. This is GENUINE BLP (income inside the log, a single constant alpha = -beta*(income_ref - anchor_price); the diminishing-marginal-utility-of-income curvature is the mechanism), NOT the earlier f-multiplier form (which froze income in the log and re-added it outside — that was not BLP). The US anchor and every at-parity number are invariant to phi (y_eff = income_ref at the US reference). Cultivated (a premium at R>1) penetrates LESS where income is lower; the effect saturates above ~US incomes (a $30 product is negligible to a high earner). phi=0 removes it; phi=1 is raw, over-steep BLP.

inputs.name: taste_quality_p
inputs.source: [Nectar] plant-based meat AVERAGE blind-taste deficit vs real meat. Nectar 'Taste of the Industry' 2025: only ~16% (20/122) of PB SKUs reach blind sensory parity, so the category average is BELOW parity. Normalised like (accept_x-1): 0 = parity, negative = deficit
inputs.note: taste is the binding constraint on PB meat (Nectar); the best ~16% reach parity, the average lags -> a modest negative, weighted by w_taste in utils.

inputs.name: w_taste
inputs.source: [calibration] taste-utility weight: converts a normalised taste gap (0=parity, -1=very poor) into utils. Large => the flavour-first mainstream punishes a taste deficit heavily; it is the single shared taste coefficient for all products. It also sets the SCALE the other perception weights are read against: taste is the #1 food-choice driver (IFIC 2025; Malone & Lusk 2017 find taste WTP ~2x health and ~3x safety), so w_taste is the largest non-price weight and health (w_health_M ~0.17x w_taste) sits well below it.

inputs.name: w_eth
inputs.source: [Gallup] ethics-driven CORE = vegetarian (4%) + vegan (1%), Gallup 2023
inputs.note: 5% is the ethics core and is KEPT. Plant-based lands at ~1% (not ~5%) because the cheap, HEALTHY whole-food outside option (the health premium w_health_E x health_w) absorbs most ethical eaters — NOT because the segment is smaller. The flexitarian PB buyer base (~89% of buyers, GFI 2024) lives in the MAINSTREAM via theta_free_M, not here.

inputs.name: w_realtissue_M
inputs.source: [calibration, SOLVED] MAINSTREAM utility weight on REAL TISSUE (=1 conventional & cultivated, =0 plant-based & whole-food). SOLVED at runtime so the mainstream carries pb_mainstream_frac (~89%) of plant-based buyers (GFI/Morning Consult 2024). The stored value is a seed.
inputs.note: A REDUCED-FORM bundle: the mainstream non-price standing of non-real-meat products (genuine 'I want real meat' preference + processed/habit residual). Cross-sectionally it is NOT separately identifiable from habit (we only observe plant-based, which lacks both), so we do not split it (Heckman state-dependence-vs-heterogeneity). HABIT proper lives in the diffusion rung (adoption_timing) + the long-run acceptance dials accept_x/theta_free_M. real_tissue is the IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTION that cultivated, being real tissue, ESCAPES this penalty (inherits conventional's standing) — the load-bearing premise, giving conventional > cultivated > plant-based at parity as a structural PREDICTION, not a fitted result.

inputs.name: pb_mainstream_frac
inputs.source: [GFI] share of plant-based-meat BUYERS who are NOT vegetarian/vegan (mainstream flexitarians/omnivores): GFI/Morning Consult 2024 (~89%: 57% omnivore + 15% flexitarian + ~17% other; only ~11% veg/vegan)
inputs.note: pins w_realtissue_M: PB's ~1.2% must be carried mostly by the MAINSTREAM (flexitarians), not the 5% ethical core. Solved jointly with the segment-specific whole-food intercepts.

inputs.name: wf_mainstream_target
inputs.source: [assumed, SOFT] mainstream 'meatless-by-choice' share: the fraction of mainstream meat-occasions where a whole-food plant protein is chosen over meat
inputs.note: pins w_health_M (the mainstream health weight) so the cheap, healthy outside option does not spill unrealistically into the mainstream. SOFT (no clean source); mostly moves the whole-food line, NOT the cultivated headline (self-check [6]: <=0.2pp). Lowered 0.10->0.06 so total whole-food (~ethical core 5pp + this) sits ~10%, not ~14%; the irreducible part is the ethical segment eating beans (w_eth * ~96% ~= 5pp), which IS the model's premise, not a free knob.

inputs.name: w_health_M
inputs.source: [calibration, SOLVED] MAINSTREAM weight on the HEALTH attribute — SOLVED so mainstream whole-food == wf_mainstream_target. Seed only. Times the whole-food health position (health_w), this is the mainstream's pull toward beans; it REPLACES the old free whole-food intercept K_wholefood_M.
inputs.note: SEGMENT-SPECIFIC (vs w_health_E for the ethical segment): mainstream meat-eaters weight health less / substitute beans for a meat occasion rarely, so this weight is much smaller than the ethical one. Splitting the health weight by segment is what lets w_realtissue_M be pinned to the buyer split without the cheap bean option leaking into the mainstream. LITERATURE CHECK: Malone & Lusk (2017, J. Agric. Appl. Econ. 49:139), a US discrete-choice experiment with taste, health and safety perceptions on a common -5..+5 scale, find WTP of $0.60/$0.31/$0.21 per unit -> mainstream HEALTH is ~0.52x TASTE (and the IFIC 2025 'very important' ratio ~0.78x brackets the soft end). The solved w_health_M lands at ~0.17x w_taste — i.e. health is weighted BELOW taste and price for the mainstream, well below the ~0.5x discrete-choice anchor.

inputs.name: w_realtissue_E
inputs.source: [assumed] ethical-segment weight on real tissue ~ 0: ethical eaters choose on slaughter-free, not on 'real meat'

inputs.name: w_slaughter_E
inputs.source: [assumed] ETHICAL-segment utility weight on the SLAUGHTER-FREE attribute (=1 for p, x, w; =0 for conventional). Large => segment E strongly avoids conventional and is drawn to no-slaughter options; this is what lets cultivated win an early beachhead at R>1

inputs.name: mk_supply_elast
inputs.source: [Brester, Marsh and Atwood 2004: 10-year supply elasticities cattle 3.24, hogs 1.8, poultry 14; Geibel et al. 2021, Table 1: simulated combined elasticities 0.4 to 4.6] long-run supply elasticity of conventional meat: with demand elasticity ed, conventional's price falls as p0 x (1 - s)^(1 / (es - ed)) when cultivated meat takes a share s of a region's meat
inputs.note: applied to each region's market as a whole: the same s, the region's share by volume, for all its kinds of meat. Solved with the share (a lower price lowers the share). Very large = a fixed price

inputs.name: mk_demand_elast
inputs.source: [USDA ERS Technical Bulletin 1956: beef -0.56, pork -0.79, chicken -0.58] own-price elasticity of demand for conventional meat in the price fall above
inputs.note: a round middle of the three

inputs.name: meat_displaced_per_kg
inputs.unit: kg of conventional meat a kg sold
inputs.source: [assumed; no study measures it for cultivated meat] kilos of conventional meat not bought for each kilo of cultivated meat sold. The model's shares are shares of the meat sold; this converts them into meat replaced: the tonnes displaced (the page's entry-point bubbles), the land animals spared (meat_market.animals_per_tonne_sold) and the fall in conventional meat's sales that lowers its price (meat_market._rollup). The shares sold do not use it, except through that price fall (a smaller fall in conventional meat's sales lowers its price less, which raises the share a little). Evidence for plant-based meat, an analogue: Winslow, Peacock, Dhargawe, Sherman, Green and Mathur 2026 (SocArXiv, doi:10.31235/osf.io/tpyk9_v1; 1.2 million US and Canadian restaurant transactions, 2016-23): plant-based meats took 1-9% of orders, yet meat orders did not measurably fall (pooled about -1%, range -15% to +16%); Hope, Green, Peacock and Mathur 2026 (Food Quality and Preference 143:105931; randomised, 4,431 US adults, an online menu): adding two plant-based options cut meat orders by 2.1 points (95% CI -4.4 to +0.1), most of their orders coming from the existing vegetarian option; grocery scanner studies (Cuffey et al. 2023, Neuhofer and Lusk 2022, Meyer et al. 2024; reviewed in Peacock 2026, Appetite 216:108301) find plant-based sales without a detectable fall in meat bought. That is close to 0 kg of meat displaced per kg of plant-based meat sold
inputs.note: 1 = every kilo sold replaces a kilo of conventional meat, what the model assumed, unstated, until 2026-11-22. Cultivated meat is meat, and the model's real-tissue attribute is why it draws its sales from conventional meat, so the near-zero figure measured for plant-based meat is not carried over; 0.5 is the low end the model allows for sales that come partly from shoppers buying more meat in all or from meals without meat (a judgement, not a measurement). Not drawn in the uncertainty bands: they are bands of the share sold, which this input moves only through conventional meat's price, and the price-fall inputs (mk_supply_elast, mk_demand_elast) are not drawn either

inputs.name: mk_closed_us_permanent
inputs.source: [US Census Vintage 2025] Florida (SB 1084, 2024), Alabama (SB 23, 2024), Mississippi (HB 1006, 2025), Montana (HB 401, 2025), Nebraska (LB 246, 2025): 34.77M of 341.78M people
inputs.note: population share as the proxy for the share of US meat eaten: no state-level figure for meat eaten a head was found, so meat a head is assumed equal between states

inputs.name: mk_closed_us_temporary
inputs.source: [US Census Vintage 2025] Texas (SB 261, to 1 Sep 2027), Indiana (HB 1425, to 30 Jun 2027), South Dakota (SB 124, 2026-2031): 39.62M people
inputs.note: population share as the proxy

inputs.name: mk_closed_eu_contested
inputs.source: [Eurostat, 1 Jan 2025; FAO food balance sheets 2023] Italy (Law 172/2023, 58.94M people at 71.2 kg of meat a head) and Hungary (Act LXXXIX of 2025, 9.54M at 76.3 kg) against the EU-27 (451.28M at 78.55 kg)
inputs.note: both contested under EU law (Italy adopted its law during the TRIS standstill; the Commission and four member states objected to Hungary's notification). By population alone it was 15.18%

inputs.name: mk_world_pop_m
inputs.source: [UN World Population Prospects 2024] world population in 2025
inputs.note: the world's meat is this times 45.12 kg a head (meat_market.MEAT_KG_HEAD)

inputs.name: mk_closed_religious_against
inputs.source: [FAO food balance sheets 2023; Our World in Data population 2023] Indonesia's meat (281.2M people at 19.95 kg a head), where the one religious body found to have ruled against cultivated meat sits: Nahdlatul Ulama, national conference of 26 Sep 2021 (secondary source)
inputs.note: the world only. All of Indonesia is counted; Nahdlatul Ulama's followers are roughly half of Indonesians (a rough figure), which gives the low end

inputs.name: mk_closed_religious_conditions
inputs.source: [FAO food balance sheets 2023, latest year for Sudan, Somalia, Mali, Chad and Brunei; Our World in Data population 2023] the meat of the populations whose religious authorities have ruled it permissible on conditions (halal or kosher donor cells, no blood or pig products in the medium, supervision): 47 Muslim-majority countries other than Indonesia, half of Nigeria, and Israel
inputs.note: the world only, and closed only if those conditions were not met. Rulings: International Islamic Fiqh Academy Resolution 265, 2025; Singapore MUIS 2024; Malaysia JAKIM 2025; Israel's Chief Rabbi 2023; OU 2023. Whole countries are counted, so non-Muslims in Muslim-majority countries are in and Muslims elsewhere (India, Europe, Russia, China) and observant Jews outside Israel are out; the range allows for both

inputs.name: mk_closed_level
inputs.source: [the brief's default] which laws close a market: 0 none; 1 permanent bans; 2 every law in force, the temporary ones and the two contested EU laws included; 3 the same and, for the world, Indonesia (mk_closed_religious_against); 4 the same and, for the world, mk_closed_religious_conditions
inputs.note: default: permanent bans only

inputs.name: pb_share_target
inputs.source: [GFI/SPINS; GFI/NIQ; derived] plant-based meat's share of TOTAL meat BY VOLUME: 0.7% of US meat dollars in 2025 and 0.8% in 2024 (GFI/SPINS), at a price 77% (2023) and 65% (2022) above meat per pound (GFI/NIQ): volume share = dollar share / price ratio = 0.7/1.77 to 0.8/1.65 = 0.35-0.45%
inputs.note: 2026-11-20: was 0.012 (1.2%), although its own note said '<1% by volume'. No direct volume figure exists: the share is derived from dollar shares and price ratios, US retail with foodservice taken alike. World about 0.3%; Germany 1-2%. The calibration ANCHOR: the whole-food health weight w_health is solved at runtime so the model reproduces this with cultivated absent (market_share.solve_calibration) — a solved calibration target, not a static floor.

inputs.name: pb_committed_share
inputs.source: [GFI/NielsenIQ 2022; Circana 2024] the share of shoppers who are the committed buyers of plant-based meat: 7% of US households made 82% of plant-based meat spending (GFI/NielsenIQ household panel, 2022). They are taken out of the mainstream segment.
inputs.note: lo: Circana's household panel (2024) has a fifth of buyers making 75% of spending; with household reach at 11% (GFI, 2025) that is about 2% of households. hi: 10%, between 7% and the 11% who buy at all in a year. Not drawn in the bands (it moves plant-based meat, not cultivated meat: research_notes/demand_checks.md section 5).

inputs.name: pb_committed_volume
inputs.source: [GFI/NielsenIQ 2022; Circana 2024] the share of the mainstream's plant-based meat that its committed buyers buy: 82% of spending by 7% of households (GFI/NielsenIQ 2022); 75% by a fifth of buyers (Circana 2024). The figure is for all households; it is applied inside the mainstream segment, which buys pb_mainstream_frac (89%) of plant-based meat.
inputs.note: Solved for through pb_committed_liking. Spending shares are taken as volume shares (the committed buyers are assumed to pay the same price a kilo as other buyers).

inputs.name: pb_committed_price_x
inputs.source: [Tonsor, Lusk & Schroeder 2021; demand_heterogeneity_evidence.md sections 3-4] how strongly the committed buyers respond to plant-based meat's price, as a multiple of other shoppers' response. In stated choices of Beyond Beef, people who do not regularly eat meat had own-price elasticities of -0.9 to -1.6, regular meat eaters -3.6 to -8.6 (a ratio of 0.10 to 0.44; of the mid-points, 0.2). Across meat and egg studies the most and least price-sensitive groups differ 4 to 10 times in real purchases (0.10 to 0.25).
inputs.note: An elasticity ratio overstates the ratio of price coefficients when the less sensitive group also buys the product more often (a logit elasticity is the coefficient times price times one minus the share), so the mode sits a little above the mid-points' 0.2, and hi at 0.5. It is a measured input, not fitted to plant-based meat's elasticity: that elasticity is the check (demand_checks.py). 1 with pb_committed_share 0 gives the model before 2026-11-21's fourth batch. Applied only to plant-based meat's price: the evidence measures these buyers' response to it, and the price-insensitive groups found for meat are the most hostile to cultivated meat (demand_heterogeneity_evidence.md section 2).

inputs.name: pb_committed_liking
inputs.source: [calibration, SOLVED] utils the committed buyers add to plant-based meat's utility, solved so they buy pb_committed_volume of the mainstream's plant-based meat. Seed only.

inputs.name: price_insensitive_share
inputs.source: [Lusk 2019 report to FFAR/FMI; Washio et al. 2023; Carzedda & Troiano 2021; demand_heterogeneity_evidence.md section 3; size fitted within that range, demand_checks.md section 7] the share of shoppers who respond much less to price than the others. Studies that split meat and egg buyers into groups find a price-insensitive group of 15-35% in stated choices (eggs 35%, Japanese beef mince 32%, Italian burgers 35%); in real purchases it is probably 8-15%.
inputs.note: FITTED within the evidence: with price_insensitive_response and the spread of liking (liking_sd, liking_tail) re-fitted, the joint misfit of the demand checks is least at 8% (1.07; 6%: 1.16, 10%: 1.14; demand_checks.md section 7), the lower end of the range for real purchases. Not drawn in the bands, like liking_sd and the committed buyers' inputs: equal_price_share is set given them. 0 gives the model before 2026-11-22's fifth batch.

inputs.name: price_insensitive_response
inputs.source: [demand_heterogeneity_evidence.md section 3; fitted within its range, demand_checks.md section 7] how strongly the price-insensitive shoppers respond to every price, as a multiple of other shoppers' response. Between the most and least price-sensitive groups, price coefficients differ 5-19 times in stated choices and probably 4-10 times in real purchases (central 6): 0.10-0.25, central 0.17.
inputs.note: FITTED within the evidence: the joint misfit of the demand checks is least at 0.11 (nine times between the groups; 0.13: 1.12, 0.15: 1.14-1.20, 0.17: 1.35, demand_checks.md section 7), near the end of the range where the price-insensitive respond least: farmed salmon's check pulls that way. Applied to both price channels (the dollar term and the ratio term) of every product, as a per-tier elasticity override is (market_share ratio_scale). Stated choices give far more: 0.036 in Washio et al. 2023 (the 'generous customers' against the weighted mean of the other four groups), 0.38 in Carzedda & Troiano 2021 (the 'Italian organic supporters' against the others), 0.08 in Lusk's eggs (the 'price insensitive' against the other three). Not drawn in the bands.

inputs.name: price_insensitive_liking
inputs.source: [Washio et al. 2023; Carzedda & Troiano 2021; demand_checks.md section 7] how much more the price-insensitive shoppers like cultivated meat than other shoppers do, in utils (negative: they like it less). In the two latent-class studies that report it, the price-insensitive group is the most hostile to cultured meat in money (willingness to pay), but not in utils: its utility for cultured over conventional meat is -1.90 against a weighted mean of -1.95 for the other groups (Washio, 4,421 Japanese shoppers) and -0.54 against -2.49 (Carzedda, 1,069 Italian students). Its hostility in money comes from its small price coefficient: a utility gap divided by a small coefficient is a large sum. The model reproduces that with a shift of 0: at a sixth of the price response, the same dislike in utils is six times as many dollars.
inputs.note: lo: hostile in utils too: Carzedda's class measured against plant-based meat rather than conventional meat (-0.43 against +0.15, about -0.6), and a margin for the possibility that part of a latent class's small price coefficient is a small scale (all of its coefficients are small in Carzedda), which would make its utils for cultured meat understate its dislike. hi: Carzedda's +1.95 against conventional meat. No study finds price-insensitive shoppers among cultured meat's enthusiasts: the enthusiast groups (13-16%) have middling or high price sensitivity. Not drawn in the bands (the mean liking is solved given it); its effect is the side table in demand_checks.md section 7.

inputs.name: w_health_E
inputs.source: [calibration, SOLVED] ETHICAL-segment weight on the HEALTH attribute — SOLVED so the ethical-segment plant-based rate hits its target (the residual ~11% of PB buyers / the non-mainstream part of pb_share_target). Times the whole-food health position (health_w), this is the ethical segment's strong pull toward whole foods; it REPLACES the old free intercept K_wholefood. Seed.
inputs.note: this (a large health weight on the healthy whole-food option), not a smaller w_eth, is why a 5% ethical core yields only ~0.1pp of PB: the healthy whole-food option (beans/tofu) absorbs most ethical eaters. Diffusion ruled out (PB is mature/declining). Mainstream uses the smaller w_health_M. The health-minded and the ethical overlap, so the ethical segment weights health heavily — the principled reason it defaults to whole foods over a processed veggie burger.

inputs.name: neophobia_x
inputs.source: [behavioural] CULTIVATED's long-run NOVELTY attitude (utility offset): NEGATIVE = food neophobia (wary of a novel/unfamiliar food — a penalty), POSITIVE = neophilia (drawn to the new — a bonus), 0 = neutral (treated like conventional on novelty). Adjustable +/-. This is the PERMANENT (long-run) part — where novelty attitude LANDS after the product is familiar; the INITIAL cold-start value neophobia_x0 fades toward THIS with exposure.
inputs.note: Default 0 is neutral and non-load-bearing. Dial NEGATIVE if a residual 'lab-grown is unnatural' aversion persists even after the product is familiar (distinct from a TASTE deficit, which is accept_x); POSITIVE if novelty / cleaner-tech is itself a draw. An exploration dial alongside accept_x and theta_free_M (Gate 2); held at 0 centrally.

inputs.name: neophobia_p
inputs.source: [behavioural] PLANT-BASED's NOVELTY attitude (utility offset; same sign convention as neophobia_x: - = neophobia, + = neophilia). An EXPLORATORY override applied after calibration (like a_p, R_p): default 0 keeps PB at its calibrated ~1.2%; move it to ask 'what if PB faced more/less novelty resistance?'. PB's residual processed-food / 'fake meat' resistance is already baked into the calibrated w_realtissue_M, so this term is a DEVIATION from that, not a double-count.
inputs.note: Lets plant-based be explored as a first-class product (with a_p, R_p). Default 0 = the observed, calibrated position; it is not in the headline band.

inputs.name: neophobia_x0
inputs.source: [DATA-ANCHORED] cultivated's INITIAL (cold-start, today) novelty attitude — the value of neophobia_x at the launch of diffusion (t=0), before any familiarity builds. It FADES with cumulative exposure (mere-exposure effect) at rate accept_rate, relaxing toward the long-run neophobia_x. DEFAULT -2.8 is anchored to data: at price+taste parity (R=1, accept_x=1) it reproduces cultivated's observed COLD at-parity share of ~5% (Van Loo, Caputo & Lusk 2020, US choice experiment: lab-grown 5% at price parity with beef). The RANGE [-3.5, +1.5] spans the full survey FRAMING band: -3.5 -> ~3% (coldest), -2.8 -> ~6% (Lusk choice exp ~5%), 0 -> ~49% (neutral), ~+0.5 -> ~60% (Perdue 2024 'cultivated chicken in a restaurant', the warmest framing), +1.5 -> ~80% (beyond the surveys). The legacy 'launch wariness' is now DERIVED = neophobia_x0 - neophobia_x (the transient part that fades).
inputs.note: Replaces the old neophobia_launch (which was the delta x0 - x_long); setting the two ENDPOINTS (initial x0, final neophobia_x) directly is more intuitive than setting the delta. Cold-start default -2.8 = 'today's unfamiliar consumer'; it sets the START of the diffusion S-curve, not the equilibrium (which is neophobia_x). With accept_x it captures the plant-based lesson: exposure cures the NOVELTY penalty (this fades), but a TASTE deficit (accept_x<1) is permanent. SWEPT in the Monte Carlo so the 5-60% framing uncertainty enters the band.

inputs.name: p_innov
inputs.source: [literature] Bass innovation coeff.; near the cross-study norm (~0.03 avg in Bass-model meta-analyses) — independent adopters
inputs.note: Bass meta-analyses (Sultan/Farley/Lehmann 1990; Van den Bulte 2002) center p~0.01-0.03; range spans slow (0.005) to fast (0.05) early uptake.

inputs.name: q_imit
inputs.source: [literature] Bass imitation coeff.; near the cross-study norm (~0.38 avg) — word-of-mouth/contagion
inputs.note: Bass meta-analytic norm q~0.3-0.5; range 0.20-0.60 spans weak to strong contagion.

inputs.name: accept_rate
inputs.source: [assumed] how fast the INITIAL neophobia (neophobia_x0) decays toward the long-run neophobia_x, per unit cumulative AVAILABILITY (rollout F, not the small consumed share)
inputs.note: UNGROUNDED (sets WHEN novelty fades, not the long-run ceiling — that is neophobia_x / accept_x / theta_free_M). ~0.15 -> ~90% faded by yr~23; range 0.05 (novelty barely resolves within 30yr) to 0.50 (fast, ~90% by yr~13). Driving it by consumed share would never ignite once shares are realistically ~1%, hence availability (F). SWEPT in the MC (time-to-stabilize uncertainty).

inputs.name: repeat_rate
inputs.source: [GFI, 'Analyzing plant-based meat and seafood sales', SPINS consumer panel to 30 Nov 2025] the share of a year's buyers of plant-based meat and seafood in the US who bought more than once: 62% in 2025, 'relatively stable' while household reach fell from about 20% (2021) to 11% (2025). Taken for cultivated meat by analogy
inputs.note: No repeat-purchase data exist for cultivated meat sold in Singapore, the US or Australia (demand_heterogeneity_evidence.md section 6). The range is a judgement around the one plant-based figure: buying twice in a year is a weak test of repeat buying, so the true share who keep buying could be lower.

inputs.name: lapse_rate
inputs.source: [derived from GFI/SPINS household reach] the share of buyers who stop buying each year: plant-based meat's US household reach fell from about 20% to 11% between 2021 and 2025, a net fall of 1 - (11/20)^(1/4) = 14% a year with the repeat rate near 62% throughout. Taken for cultivated meat by analogy
inputs.note: The net fall understates the gross rate if lapsed buyers came back, and a fad unwinding (2019-21) overstates the rate of a settled product; the two pull in opposite directions. lo: a settled product; hi: about twice the plant-based figure.

inputs.name: milestone_year_breakthrough
inputs.source: [assumed] year a scale-up / cheaper-media breakthrough lands, stepping R down (Rung 4 cost-path coupling)
inputs.note: The WHEN of the cost step (the declared unknown), not the whether. The R endpoints of each cost path are DERIVED from the cost model (adoption_timing.COST_PATHS), not hand-typed here, so they cannot drift from Rung 2.

inputs.name: biomass_cost_nearterm
inputs.source: [derived] near-term achievable biomass: the default with medium at $0.20/L (30.5 x 0.20 + 19.1)

inputs.name: scaffold_frac
inputs.source: [assumed; products: structuring_cost.md] share of a cut that is plant-protein matrix and binder rather than cells. 0.2 keeps the cut mostly cells, the product the shopper model describes. Whole cuts sold or approved so far are 10-30% cells (Aleph 10-20%, Upside 'double-digit'); no cut that is mostly suspension-grown cells has been shown to have the texture of meat
inputs.note: Drawn in the bands (MC_CUT_INPUTS) since 2026-11-19. It sets the cut's cost (price_ratio.structured_cost) AND how much shoppers like it: a cut that is part plant protein gets that much less of the real-meat credit (meat_market.tier_offset).

inputs.name: material_price
inputs.source: [TVP, extrusion, binders: structuring_cost.md] price of the matrix: textured or extruded plant protein $0.7-2.8/kg all in (GFI 2021), TVP $0.5-5.6/kg dry (Tridge), binders $0.1-0.6/kg of product

inputs.name: process_cost
inputs.source: [analogues: structuring_cost.md] what assembling a cut costs ON TOP OF the forming, packing and quality control every product already pays in the shop add-on (au_processing, about $1): binding, setting, slicing, extra packing and yield loss. All-in estimates are $1-8 a kilo (plant-protein extrusion $0.44-1.58, surimi forming about $1, batch forming and tighter hygiene more), central $3; less the $1 already counted. Growing tissue on a scaffold in a second bioreactor would add about $10 (3-35), the route companies dropped
inputs.note: widest input on a cut; the cell share (scaffold_frac) is the larger unknown. Drawn in the bands (MC_CUT_INPUTS) since 2026-11-19.

inputs.name: p_conv_premium_fish
inputs.source: [market] premium fish / BlueNalu target

inputs.name: p_conv_sushi_salmon
inputs.source: [market] sushi-grade salmon / Wildtype target

inputs.name: ts_ph_relaxed
inputs.source: [derived, research_notes/gas_exchange_study.md section 8] the alkaline dose a column loop may give the culture in the what-if that relaxes the pH check: the safe design (55 mbar out, 0.5 m3 of loop in a 20 m3 tank) is 0.29 of the dose that slowed CHO cells, so twice it is 0.58
inputs.note: 3.4 times the safe dose is the dose that slowed CHO cells (Paul et al. 2020, via a summary); one study, inferred measure of 'rise x share'

inputs.name: ts_loop_hw_exp
inputs.source: [assumed] how fast the cost of the retention loop's hardware per m2 of membrane falls with tank size, in the what-if that gives it economies of scale: per m2 it scales as (V/20)^-0.3, so the hardware as a whole scales as V^0.7
inputs.note: the base model prices every m2 alike (rt_tff_hw); pumps, housings and controls cost less per m2 in a bigger skid and more in a small one; the membranes themselves do not change. The usual exponent for process equipment is 0.6 to 0.7 (ge_vessel_cost_exp is 0.6)

inputs.name: ts_hazard_exp
inputs.source: [assumed] how fast the chance of losing a run per tank-day grows with tank size, in the what-if that makes it grow: hazard x (V/20)^0.333
inputs.note: the base model holds the chance per tank-day fixed. A bigger tank has more ports, seals and connections (surface goes as V^(2/3)) and a loss costs the whole tank, so the loss per kilo rises with the chance per tank-day. No source gives it by tank size; BioPlan's survey found larger facilities had about three times the contamination of smaller ones (facilities, not tanks)

inputs.name: tc_phi_max
inputs.source: [Iordan, Duperray and Verdier 2007, arXiv:0709.3671, read in full] the maximum packing in the Krieger-Dougherty fit to the viscosity of CHO suspensions at 1,000 per second (eta/eta0 = (1 - phi/phi0)^(-2.5 phi0))
inputs.note: 0.64 is random close packing of hard spheres, 0.74 the face-centred cubic limit. Their cells were spun down and re-diluted at 20 C and not growing

inputs.name: tc_thin
inputs.source: [Tregidgo et al. 2023, Chem Eng Res Des 194:344, read in full] CHO at 1e8 cells/mL, 37 C: 2.4 mPa s at 50 rpm in a 250 mL tank against 1.8 at a shear rate of 45 per second (the viscosity the Thomas equation gives for a quarter cells by volume): the excess viscosity is 1.33 times higher at the low shear a large tank has
inputs.note: hi: the same paper, 'viscosities increase up to 3-fold ... at shear rates below 40 per second', with high scatter. Applied to the excess of the suspension over the medium

inputs.name: tc_kla_exp
inputs.source: [Yagi and Yoshida 1975, as listed in a university course note, snippet] the oxygen transfer coefficient falls with the apparent viscosity to the power -0.40 in stirred tanks of Newtonian and non-Newtonian liquids
inputs.note: lo: Amgen's CHO perfusion cultures at 1e5 to 35e5 cells/mL lost almost no kLa (AIChE 2017 abstract, 403 on fetch) and Pappenreiter saw none between cell-free and spent harvest medium (via Bioprocess Intl 2024). hi: a 2025 Biotechnology Journal paper reports a 10-40% fall with culture rheology (snippet, not read). Humbird's kLa equation has no viscosity term

inputs.name: tc_np
inputs.source: [Tregidgo et al. 2023, read in full] power number of the dual-impeller 250 mL tank, 4.9; elephant-ear and pitched-blade impellers in large tanks run at 1.3-1.5 (assumed)
inputs.note: at a fixed power per volume a lower power number turns the stirrer faster and raises the Reynolds number, so 5 is the cautious end

inputs.name: tc_re_turb
inputs.source: [Tregidgo et al. 2023, read in full] a mixing number (time x speed) that stays constant from Re 5,600 up; the usual boundary of fully turbulent flow is 10,000
inputs.note: above this Reynolds number, Humbird's mixing-time equation (which has no viscosity in it) holds

inputs.name: tc_bubble_mm
inputs.source: [research_notes/gas_flow_cap.md, section 3, citing a bubble-column measurement in synthetic medium with poloxamer] bubbles of 3-4 mm

inputs.name: tc_holdup
inputs.source: [research_notes/gas_flow_cap.md, section 3] gas hold-up at 6 mm/s: 3.5% at 4.2 mm/s and 4.5% at 7.7 mm/s
inputs.note: measured without cells, at the viscosity of the medium

inputs.name: tc_yield_sigma
inputs.source: [Iordan, Duperray and Verdier 2007, read in full] the stress scale sigma* of the fractal-aggregate fit to their yield stresses
inputs.note: their Figure 4a values were not extracted; the yield stress is taken as sigma* (phi/phi0)^m, with m below. They fitted CHO at 20 C, spun down and re-diluted

inputs.name: tc_yield_exp
inputs.source: [Iordan, Duperray and Verdier 2007, read in full] yield stress grows as phi to the power 8.4

inputs.name: tc_peak_dissipation
inputs.source: [Humbird 2021, Eq. 2.17 after Nienow 2010, read in part] the energy dissipation near the impeller against the tank average

inputs.name: tc_jacket_u
inputs.source: [assumed] heat transfer through the wall of a jacketed steel tank holding a thick culture, inside film included
inputs.note: textbook range for a stirred jacketed vessel; nothing found for a 20 m3 animal-cell tank

inputs.name: tc_cool_dt
inputs.source: [assumed] temperature difference between the culture (37 C) and the cooling water in the jacket

inputs.name: ml_dry_mol_kg
inputs.source: [Humbird-R, derived] moles of dry cell mass in a kg of wet cells
inputs.note: 300 g dry matter per kg wet over 22.06 g/mol for CH1.68 O0.34 N0.21 (his Table 2.1); the figure that turns pf_nh3_efficient from per mole of dry mass into per kg

inputs.name: ml_n_per_dry
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Table 2.1: nitrogen in the cell formula CH1.68 O0.34 N0.21
inputs.note: x 13.6 = 2.86 mol N per kg wet. A protein-only count gives about 2.2 (195 g protein per kg wet at 16% nitrogen); nucleic acids add about 0.2

inputs.name: ml_aa_pure_kg
inputs.source: [Humbird-R] Table 3.4: pure amino acids the cells take up per kg of wet cells (Reaction 2.11); quoted in the aa_intensity note
inputs.note: free amino acids in the proportion the cell builds protein; the hydrolysate (0.337) carries more because its profile does not match

inputs.name: ml_aa_mw
inputs.source: [textbook] mean molar mass of a free amino acid: 110 for a protein residue plus 18 for water

inputs.name: ml_glc_mw
inputs.source: [textbook] glucose

inputs.name: ml_salts_osm
inputs.source: [judgement; research_notes/min_litres_per_kg.md] osmolality of the salts and buffer in a conventional medium, without its glucose and amino acids
inputs.note: about 100 mM NaCl (190), 25 mM bicarbonate (50) and the rest (10). Not sourced from a medium sheet. Lower values mean cells that tolerate less sodium; no source on how low the salts can go. Used only where the medium is what the cells sit in (min_litres.bounds, 'bath')

inputs.name: ml_feed_g_l
inputs.source: [judgement; research_notes/min_litres_per_kg.md] strength of a concentrated feed of amino acids and glucose, as solids per litre, that is mixed into the tank and diluted there
inputs.note: single-strength perfusion media carry roughly 10-30 g/L of these (unsourced); feeds of 5-10 times that are used in fed-batch (the search found papers on ultra-concentrated feeds, limited by tyrosine and cystine solubility, and no figure). No measurement in a 20 m3 perfusion tank

inputs.name: ml_nh3_chogs
inputs.source: [Mayrhofer et al. 2020, via waste_tricks_sizing.md B2, derived] ammonia of a glutamine-synthetase CHO line in optimised perfusion, if its 0.54 fmol per cell per hour held at 0.35 per day
inputs.note: the lowest ammonia in any source read. Measured in cells that were not growing; the extrapolation to faster growth is an inference, and the cells are CHO, not meat cells

inputs.name: ml_atp_bio
inputs.source: [Kilburn, Lilly and Webb 1969, J Cell Sci 4:645, via the BioNumbers page (ID 101985), read]: ATP to build a mouse fibroblast (LS cell)
inputs.note: cell size not given on that page; used only as a cross-check on the oxygen the model burns

inputs.name: ml_atp_maint
inputs.source: [Kilburn et al. 1969, as above] ATP for upkeep per new cell at a 1.15 day generation time

inputs.name: ml_kilburn_td_h
inputs.source: [Kilburn et al. 1969] the 1.15 day generation time of that upkeep figure

inputs.name: gb_conc_insulin
inputs.source: [Humbird-R Sect. 3.1, FT; GFI 2023 footnote 4, FT; Chen et al. 2011 Essential 8] insulin in the medium: 19.4 mg/L

inputs.name: gb_conc_transferrin
inputs.source: [Humbird-R Sect. 3.1, FT; GFI 2023 footnote 4, FT] transferrin: 10.7 mg/L

inputs.name: gb_conc_fgf
inputs.source: [Humbird-R Sect. 3.1, FT; GFI 2023 footnote 4, FT] FGF: 0.1 mg/L

inputs.name: gb_conc_tgfb
inputs.source: [Humbird-R Sect. 3.1, FT; GFI 2023 footnote 4, FT] TGF-beta: 0.002 mg/L

inputs.name: gb_price_insulin
